questions.question: Around 600 BC the kingdom of Lydia (in modern Turkey) under King Alyattes minted the first standardized coins from electrum, a natural gold-silver alloy from the Pactolus River. Each coin carried a lion-head stamp guaranteeing weight and purity. Herodotus credited the Lydians with inventing both coinage and retail trade. Why was the Lydian innovation so consequential?
questions.answer: A trusted standardized unit of account collapsed transaction costs, letting trade scale beyond personal acquaintance for the first time
choices: A trusted standardized unit of account collapsed transaction costs, letting trade scale beyond personal acquaintance for the first time
Coinage failed quickly because merchants preferred barter and refused to accept the Lydian electrum stamps in any large transactions
The Lydian coins were declared illegal by neighboring Greek city-states which banned all standardized currency for several centuries afterward
Coinage was meaningless until Rome formalized it in 200 BC and the Lydian experiment had no measurable effect on Mediterranean trade
questions.context: Croesus of Lydia (~560 BC) refined the system into pure-gold and pure-silver coins. Greek city-states adopted coinage almost immediately, and the practice spread across the Mediterranean.

questions.question: From roughly 1870 to 1914 the major industrial economies operated on the classical gold standard. Each currency was defined as a fixed weight of gold, central banks redeemed notes for gold on demand, and capital moved freely across borders. The era produced unprecedented economic integration, falling consumer prices, and roughly 3.5% real US growth. What ended it?
questions.answer: World War I, when belligerent governments suspended gold convertibility to print money for wartime spending, and the system never fully recovered
choices: World War I, when belligerent governments suspended gold convertibility to print money for wartime spending, and the system never fully recovered
The Wall Street Crash of 1929, where equity markets collapsed and forced every nation off the gold standard simultaneously within only a few weeks
A scientific consensus among economists in 1910 that gold was an outdated metal unfit for backing any modern industrial-era national currency anywhere
The discovery of new gold deposits in South Africa in 1886 which made the metal so abundant that it lost all its monetary value worldwide for years
questions.context: Britain returned to gold in 1925 at the pre-war parity (Churchill's decision, criticized by Keynes); the gold-exchange standard staggered through the 1930s and was effectively dead by 1936.

questions.question: At Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, in July 1944, 730 delegates from 44 Allied nations negotiated the postwar monetary order. John Maynard Keynes proposed a global reserve currency called the 'bancor' issued by an International Clearing Union. Harry Dexter White of the US Treasury proposed pegging currencies to the dollar, which alone would be redeemable in gold at $35/oz. Whose plan won?
questions.answer: White's, because the US held about two-thirds of world gold reserves and was the only major economy not devastated by war, so it dictated the terms
choices: White's, because the US held about two-thirds of world gold reserves and was the only major economy not devastated by war, so it dictated the terms
Keynes's, because his prestige as the world's most famous economist forced the US delegation to adopt the bancor scheme over American objections at Bretton
A compromise plan from France that synthesized the British and American proposals and was adopted unanimously after three days of debate among delegates
Neither, because the conference ended in deadlock and the postwar monetary system was actually designed by the IMF staff in 1946 after the fact ended
questions.context: Harry Dexter White was later identified in Venona decrypts as having passed information to Soviet intelligence. The Bretton Woods system began functioning ~1958 and lasted until Nixon closed the gold window August 15, 1971.

questions.question: In 1960 Belgian-American economist Robert Triffin warned the US Senate of a contradiction in Bretton Woods. The world needed dollars for trade and reserves, which meant the US had to run persistent deficits to supply them. But persistent deficits would eventually destroy confidence in dollar-gold convertibility. He predicted the system would collapse. What was he describing?
questions.answer: The Triffin dilemma, in which a reserve-currency issuer cannot simultaneously supply global liquidity and maintain confidence in its currency's value
choices: The Triffin dilemma, in which a reserve-currency issuer cannot simultaneously supply global liquidity and maintain confidence in its currency's value
The trade deficit puzzle, in which countries running deficits should logically see their currencies appreciate due to capital inflows from abroad immediately
The optimal currency area problem, in which currency unions only work when labor moves freely across the regions sharing the same currency unit always
The impossible trinity, in which a country cannot have a fixed exchange rate and free capital flow and an independent monetary policy at the same time
questions.context: Triffin's prediction was vindicated when Nixon closed the gold window in 1971. His warning was given to a Senate subcommittee in 1959-60. The dilemma still applies to the post-1971 dollar system in a softer form.

questions.question: Through the 1960s, French president Charles de Gaulle accused the US of running deficits whose costs Europe was forced to absorb via dollar reserves of dubious gold backing. On his order France systematically swapped dollar holdings for US gold at the $35/oz Bretton Woods price, shipping the metal home. The US gold stockpile fell from ~20,000 tons in 1950 to under 9,000 by 1971. What did this expose?
questions.answer: Far more dollars existed worldwide than gold to redeem them at the official price, so Bretton Woods was already insolvent before Nixon closed the window
choices: Far more dollars existed worldwide than gold to redeem them at the official price, so Bretton Woods was already insolvent before Nixon closed the window
France's gold reserves were inadequate to back the franc and the redemptions were an attempt to hide French monetary weakness from observers worldwide
The US Mint had been secretly producing fake gold bars and de Gaulle's redemptions were intended to expose the counterfeiting operation publicly to all
European central banks were colluding to corner the gold market and de Gaulle's actions were rejected by other European leaders as destabilizing the system
questions.context: De Gaulle's economic adviser Jacques Rueff was an Austrian-aligned classical-liberal economist who argued for a return to a genuine gold standard. The 1960s gold drain accelerated through 1971; Nixon's closure made the underlying insolvency formal.

questions.question: On Sunday August 15, 1971, Nixon interrupted the popular show Bonanza to announce his New Economic Policy: a 90-day wage and price freeze, a 10% import surcharge, and 'temporary' suspension of dollar-gold convertibility. Treasury Secretary John Connally told European finance ministers, 'The dollar is our currency, but it's your problem.' Why did Nixon also impose wage and price controls?
questions.answer: To suppress the inflation that closing the gold window would unleash, though controls didn't work and inflation ran into double digits through the 1970s anyway
choices: To suppress the inflation that closing the gold window would unleash, though controls didn't work and inflation ran into double digits through the 1970s anyway
To stabilize the US dollar's value against foreign currencies through direct administrative pricing of goods sold in international markets after the closure
To prevent labor unions from striking during the 1972 election year, since strikes would have damaged Nixon's domestic political position before the vote
To reduce the federal deficit, since wage and price controls increase tax revenue by raising nominal incomes faster than nominal expenditures over time
questions.context: The wage-price controls were administered by a Cost of Living Council under Donald Rumsfeld. They produced shortages, gas lines, and the 'WIN' (Whip Inflation Now) buttons that became Ford-era jokes. Volcker's 1979 rate hikes finally broke the inflation.

questions.question: Postwar Hungary in 1946 ran the largest hyperinflation ever recorded. Prices doubled every ~15 hours. The government issued the 100-quintillion-pengo note (the number 10^20, written as 100,000,000,000,000,000,000 pengo). Workers were paid daily and rushed to spend before lunch. In July 1946 the pengo was replaced by the forint at an exchange rate of 4 followed by 29 zeros pengo per forint. What caused this?
questions.answer: Soviet occupation costs paid by Hungarian printing presses on Stalin's orders, so the central bank surrendered to political demand to monetize unlimited claims
choices: Soviet occupation costs paid by Hungarian printing presses on Stalin's orders, so the central bank surrendered to political demand to monetize unlimited claims
An unusually poor wheat harvest in 1945 which reduced food supply across Hungary and pushed prices upward in a self-reinforcing spiral lasting all year
Counterfeit pengo notes printed by Western intelligence services to destabilize the Soviet-aligned government during the early Cold War years in Europe
A speculative attack by London-based currency traders who shorted the pengo on the Vienna foreign exchange market during late 1945 and early 1946 markets
questions.context: The 1946 Hungarian hyperinflation dwarfs Weimar 1923 and Zimbabwe 2008 by orders of magnitude. The forint replacement was administered by economist Béla Imrédy and stabilized only because the printing stopped.

questions.question: By November 1923, Weimar Germany's mark had collapsed. A dollar bought 4.2 trillion marks, workers were paid twice daily and ran to spend before prices doubled, and pensioners' savings were wiped out. On November 15, 1923, the Reichsbank under Hjalmar Schacht introduced the Rentenmark, backed nominally by mortgages on German land. The new currency held its value. What was the actual mechanism?
questions.answer: Schacht stopped the printing presses and committed to a strict issuance limit, so the 'land backing' was largely symbolic but the monetary discipline was real
choices: Schacht stopped the printing presses and committed to a strict issuance limit, so the 'land backing' was largely symbolic but the monetary discipline was real
German farmland was physically pledged to the Reichsbank, and farmers could be evicted if the new currency lost its purchasing power against gold reserves
The Rentenmark was secretly backed by US gold reserves transferred to Germany under a confidential 1923 agreement with the Federal Reserve System Board
British banks guaranteed the Rentenmark's value through an emergency Bank of England credit line that remained in place through the 1930s with Germany
questions.context: Hjalmar Schacht's reputation as a monetary technician was made by the Rentenmark stabilization. He later served as Hitler's economics minister and was acquitted at Nuremberg. The Reichsmark replaced the Rentenmark in 1924.

questions.question: Zimbabwe's 2008-2009 hyperinflation peaked at an estimated 89.7 sextillion percent month-on-month in November 2008. The Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe under Gideon Gono issued the 100-trillion-dollar note. The currency was abandoned in April 2009 and Zimbabweans switched to US dollars and South African rand. What policy triggered the collapse?
questions.answer: Mugabe's 2000 land seizures destroyed agricultural output, collapsing tax revenue, so the central bank monetized deficits to keep paying political loyalists
choices: Mugabe's 2000 land seizures destroyed agricultural output, collapsing tax revenue, so the central bank monetized deficits to keep paying political loyalists
An IMF structural-adjustment program imposed in 2007 which required Zimbabwe to liberalize its currency overnight against its central bank's official wishes
A regional drought in 2008 which reduced agricultural output by a small percentage and caused brief shortages of basic foodstuffs in some urban areas only
Currency speculation by traders at the Johannesburg Stock Exchange who shorted the Zimbabwe dollar during the 2008 global financial crisis period at length
questions.context: The land seizures targeted white commercial farmers; the resulting collapse in food production turned Zimbabwe from a regional food exporter into a famine importer. Gideon Gono's memoir Zimbabwe's Casino Economy (2008) blames sanctions; the monetary record blames the printing press.

questions.question: Saifedean Ammous's The Bitcoin Standard (2018) became the canonical popular case for Bitcoin as sound money. Ammous draws on Austrian monetary theory (Menger 1892 on money's origin, Mises 1912 on regression, Hayek 1976 on denationalization) to argue Bitcoin succeeds where prior digital-money attempts failed. What is his central argument about Bitcoin's hardness?
questions.answer: Bitcoin has the highest stock-to-flow ratio of any monetary asset and the most credible supply schedule in monetary history, properties gold approximated but Bitcoin perfects
choices: Bitcoin has the highest stock-to-flow ratio of any monetary asset and the most credible supply schedule in monetary history, properties gold approximated but Bitcoin perfects
Bitcoin's value comes from its anonymous founder Satoshi Nakamoto, whose identity Ammous claims to have personally verified through extensive unpublished private correspondence
Bitcoin is destined to replace the US dollar by the year 2030 according to Ammous's mathematical model based on adoption curves of past technologies he documents
Bitcoin succeeds because every transaction requires approval by a council of 21 elected miners distributed across continents to ensure global representation always
questions.context: Ammous teaches at the Lebanese American University and worked on early Bitcoin economics. The book has been translated into 30+ languages. Lyn Alden's Broken Money (2023) and Nik Bhatia's Layered Money (2021) complement Ammous as canonical popular references.

questions.question: Venezuela holds the world's largest proven oil reserves. Hugo Chavez nationalized the oil industry beginning 2007, expelled experienced engineers, and used oil revenues to fund a vast social program. When oil prices crashed in 2014 under his successor Nicolas Maduro, the bolivar collapsed. By 2018 annual inflation passed 1,000,000%. Millions fled. What does the Venezuelan record demonstrate?
questions.answer: A resource-rich country can be reduced to mass starvation by central planning and currency debasement, even sitting on the world's largest oil reserves
choices: A resource-rich country can be reduced to mass starvation by central planning and currency debasement, even sitting on the world's largest oil reserves
US sanctions in 2017 caused the Venezuelan collapse single-handedly, with no measurable contribution from Chavez or Maduro's nationalization or printing policies
Falling oil prices alone caused the crisis, since no policy choices by the government had any measurable effect on the bolivar's loss of purchasing power
Venezuela's collapse was an isolated regional anomaly with no broader lessons for monetary or development economics anywhere else outside Latin America itself
questions.context: PDVSA (the state oil company) output fell from about 3.5 million barrels per day in 1998 to under 400,000 by 2020. The exodus, estimated at over 7 million Venezuelans by 2023, is the largest displacement in modern Latin American history.

questions.question: Argentina entered the 20th century among the world's ten richest economies per capita. By 2024 it had defaulted on sovereign debt nine times, run hyperinflation in the late 1980s (Alfonsin), collapsed under a currency board in 2001-02 (de la Rua), and reached 200%+ annual inflation by 2023. The common thread across a century: Peronist fiscal expansion financed by central-bank money printing. What does Argentina illustrate?
questions.answer: A wealthy country can run itself into perpetual currency crisis through Peronist deficit spending, money printing, and political resistance to fiscal discipline
choices: A wealthy country can run itself into perpetual currency crisis through Peronist deficit spending, money printing, and political resistance to fiscal discipline
Argentina's poverty is entirely caused by IMF austerity programs imposed externally against Argentine wishes during the late 20th and early 21st centuries
Argentina's geographic isolation from major trading partners is responsible for its century of decline, and no monetary or fiscal choices had any noticeable effect
Argentina remains a wealthy economy with normal monetary conditions, and reports of its century-long decline are exaggerated political claims by foreign critics
questions.context: Javier Milei, an Austrian-school economist, was elected president in November 2023 on an explicit promise to dollarize and abolish the central bank. His first year produced sharp inflation declines and a fiscal surplus, but the political durability of the reform is open.

questions.question: Lebanon's banking system collapsed beginning 2019-2020. Banque du Liban under governor Riad Salameh ran an unsustainable currency peg and a Ponzi-like dollar-deposit scheme. The Lebanese pound lost about 98% of its value by 2023, savings were frozen, and middle-class families queued at ATMs for capped withdrawals worth pennies. The August 4, 2020 Beirut port explosion (ammonium nitrate stored since 2013) compounded the misery. What was the underlying cause?
questions.answer: A central-bank scheme paying high dollar yields with new depositor dollars (Ponzi structure) that collapsed when foreign inflows stopped, exposing decades of state capture
choices: A central-bank scheme paying high dollar yields with new depositor dollars (Ponzi structure) that collapsed when foreign inflows stopped, exposing decades of state capture
Israeli economic warfare against Lebanon caused the 2019 collapse, with no measurable contribution from any actions by Lebanese banks or the central bank itself
A regional drought across the Eastern Mediterranean in 2019 reduced agricultural output and caused the crisis through food-price shocks rather than monetary failure
The Lebanese banking system remained sound through 2023, with the currency depreciation entirely caused by speculation by London-based currency traders short the pound
questions.context: Riad Salameh was governor 1993-2023 and is wanted in multiple European jurisdictions on embezzlement and money laundering charges. Hezbollah's parallel finance and economic role complicates any clean diagnosis but does not exonerate the formal central bank.

questions.question: Jeff Booth's The Price of Tomorrow (2020) argues that the natural state of a technology-driven economy is DEFLATION, not inflation. As computing, energy, AI, and robotics drive costs down, prices SHOULD fall and purchasing power rise. Central banks fight this with money printing to engineer 2% inflation, transferring wealth to asset holders. What is Booth's policy implication?
questions.answer: Allow deflation to happen, let purchasing power rise, and replace fiat money with sound money (gold or Bitcoin) so technology benefits savers rather than the financially closest to the central bank
choices: Allow deflation to happen, let purchasing power rise, and replace fiat money with sound money (gold or Bitcoin) so technology benefits savers rather than the financially closest to the central bank
Maintain the 2% inflation target indefinitely, since deflation is dangerous and any decline in measured consumer prices causes uncontrolled spirals into a downturn
Adopt Modern Monetary Theory and run permanent fiscal deficits to absorb deflationary pressures, with no concern for currency value or for savers' real returns
Implement universal basic income funded by direct central-bank money printing, since technology will eliminate most jobs by 2030 and consumption must be supported
questions.context: Booth, a Canadian entrepreneur, frames the central-bank inflation regime as wealth redistribution from labor + savers to asset holders. The Cantillon effect is implicit throughout. The book has become a popular Bitcoin community reference.

questions.question: The stock-to-flow ratio (S/F) measures monetary hardness: existing supply divided by annual new production. Gold's S/F is about 60 (existing stockpile lasts 60 years at current mining). Bitcoin's S/F doubles every halving (about 26 in 2020, 52 in 2024). PlanB's 2019 stock-to-flow model predicted Bitcoin price from S/F. What is the legitimate insight, regardless of the model's price-prediction track record?
questions.answer: Bitcoin's supply growth is more predictable and lower than gold's after the next halvings, so its monetary hardness on the most-relevant metric exceeds gold's measurable hardness
choices: Bitcoin's supply growth is more predictable and lower than gold's after the next halvings, so its monetary hardness on the most-relevant metric exceeds gold's measurable hardness
The stock-to-flow ratio is meaningless because it doesn't account for industrial gold demand or the velocity of money or any of the standard monetary aggregates used by central banks
Stock-to-flow proves Bitcoin will reach $1 million by 2030 since the model has been confirmed by every halving cycle to date with no observable deviation from its predictions
Stock-to-flow only applies to commodity currencies like gold, since cryptocurrencies have no physical supply and the metric cannot be defined for digital assets at all
questions.context: PlanB's S/F model became famous in Bitcoin circles 2019-2021. Critics including Vitalik Buterin pointed out that the model's price predictions degrade outside the training period. The underlying hardness insight survives the price-prediction critique.

questions.question: Executive Order 6102, signed by FDR on April 5, 1933, required US citizens to surrender gold coins, bullion, and certificates to the Federal Reserve at $20.67/oz, with criminal penalties for non-compliance. After the seizure, FDR revalued gold to $35/oz in the Gold Reserve Act of 1934, instantly devaluing the dollar's gold backing by ~41%. What was the move's effect on US savers?
questions.answer: Savers who complied lost 41% of their purchasing power overnight to the federal government, a forced wealth transfer from the public to the Treasury
choices: Savers who complied lost 41% of their purchasing power overnight to the federal government, a forced wealth transfer from the public to the Treasury
Savers gained value because the gold revaluation increased the dollar's purchasing power against gold and other commodities for several years afterward
There was no wealth effect because gold and the dollar both lost value proportionally and savers' real positions were unchanged from before the executive order
Most savers ignored the order with no enforcement, and the gold confiscation existed mainly on paper and produced no measurable change in personal wealth holdings
questions.context: EO 6102's $10,000 fine (1933 dollars) plus 10 years prison was enforced via grand juries; one prominent case (Frederick Barber Campbell) ended in dismissal on procedural grounds. The ban on private US gold ownership was repealed by President Ford on December 31, 1974.

questions.question: Between 1837 and 1862 the US operated without a central bank under the 'free banking' system. State-chartered banks issued their own notes, redeemable in gold or silver, subject to state-level reserve requirements. The era is often called 'wildcat banking' in textbooks, suggesting chaos. Modern scholarship (Hugh Rockoff, George Selgin) reaches a different verdict. What does the evidence show?
questions.answer: Free banking worked better than its reputation, with most state systems running stably and bank failure rates comparable to or lower than those under later central-bank regimes
choices: Free banking worked better than its reputation, with most state systems running stably and bank failure rates comparable to or lower than those under later central-bank regimes
Free banking was catastrophic across all states with universal bank failures and total economic collapse forcing Congress to create the Federal Reserve System urgently
Free banking caused the Civil War by destabilizing the financial system to the point where political conflict became inevitable across the entire union by 1860
Free banking had no measurable economic effects, since most Americans during this period used barter and personal IOUs rather than any bank notes or coins regularly
questions.context: Selgin's The Theory of Free Banking (1988) and Rockoff's research are the canonical revisionist accounts. The 1863 National Banking Acts (Civil War financing) ended the free-banking era. The 1913 Federal Reserve Act ended the National Banking system.

questions.question: From 1716 to 1845, Scotland operated a free banking system with no central bank. Private banks issued competing banknotes redeemable in gold, with shareholders bearing unlimited liability. The Bank of Scotland (1695), Royal Bank of Scotland (1727), and dozens of others competed without crisis until the Bank Charter Act of 1844-45 brought Scotland under London's central-banking framework. Lawrence White's research is the modern reference. What does the Scottish record show?
questions.answer: A free banking system with full convertibility, branch banking, and competitive note issuance was stable for 130 years, surpassing the contemporary Bank of England's record
choices: A free banking system with full convertibility, branch banking, and competitive note issuance was stable for 130 years, surpassing the contemporary Bank of England's record
Scottish free banking was a brief experiment lasting only a few decades before being voluntarily replaced with a centralized Scottish national bank during the 1700s
Scotland never had free banking and the Bank of Scotland always had a monopoly on note issuance throughout the period under Scottish royal charter from the start
Scottish free banking ended in catastrophe in 1844 with mass bank failures, which is why English authorities had to intervene to impose central banking from London urgently
questions.context: Lawrence White's Free Banking in Britain (1984) made the Scottish case widely known among economists. Adam Smith praised the Scottish system in Wealth of Nations (1776). The 1844-45 acts were a political imposition, not a response to Scottish banking instability.

questions.question: The Continental Congress financed the American Revolution by printing 'Continentals', a paper currency unbacked by specie. By 1781 about $241 million in Continentals were outstanding against a metallic dollar value of only a few cents. The phrase 'not worth a Continental' entered English as a synonym for worthless. What lesson did the Founders draw?
questions.answer: Paper money issued by a government will be over-issued when fiscal pressure rises, so the Constitution explicitly empowered Congress only to 'coin money' (gold and silver), not print it
choices: Paper money issued by a government will be over-issued when fiscal pressure rises, so the Constitution explicitly empowered Congress only to 'coin money' (gold and silver), not print it
Paper money is always safer than coined money since paper can be replaced when damaged, while gold and silver coins lose value when worn down by extended circulation
The Continental currency was actually a great success and the new United States adopted it as the official national currency in the original Articles of Confederation
The Founders viewed the Continental currency as having no monetary effects whatsoever, and the Constitution makes no reference to coinage or paper money anywhere in its text
questions.context: Article I Section 10 of the Constitution forbids the STATES from making anything but gold and silver a tender in payment of debts. The federal government's authority to issue paper money was a later 19th-century interpretation, contested at the time.

questions.question: In 1789 the French Revolutionary government issued 'assignats', paper notes initially backed by confiscated Church lands. The Assembly promised to limit the issue. They broke the promise. By 1796 about 45 billion assignats were outstanding against shrinking land collateral; the notes traded at under 1% of face. Hyperinflation devastated wages and savings. What is the assignat episode's lesson?
questions.answer: Even land-backed paper money fails when the issuing political body cannot resist the temptation to print more during a fiscal emergency
choices: Even land-backed paper money fails when the issuing political body cannot resist the temptation to print more during a fiscal emergency
Land-backed paper money is uniquely stable and the assignat episode succeeded in financing the Revolutionary war effort without notable inflation throughout the period
The assignats failed only because of British counterfeiting, with no measurable contribution from the French Assembly's own issuance decisions to monetary depreciation
The assignat episode is unique to revolutionary France and has no broader implications for monetary economics in any other country at any other time period anywhere
questions.context: Andrew Dickson White's Fiat Money Inflation in France (1896) is the classic English-language account. Napoleon, on coming to power 1799-1804, restored a metallic franc — the political stabilization required by the monetary one.

questions.question: The Roman denarius began under Augustus at about 95% silver. By the reign of Gallienus (260-268 AD), the silver content was under 5%. Coins were physically clipped and recast smaller each generation. The Crisis of the Third Century saw inflation, sacked cities, and political chaos. Emperor Diocletian's Edict on Maximum Prices (301 AD) made it a capital offense to charge above set prices. What happened?
questions.answer: Goods disappeared from markets, black markets flourished, and the underlying problem (currency debasement) was never solved by the price controls
choices: Goods disappeared from markets, black markets flourished, and the underlying problem (currency debasement) was never solved by the price controls
The price edict succeeded and stabilized the empire's economy for centuries, with no further inflation recorded in the surviving epigraphic evidence after 301 AD
Diocletian's edict had no measurable effect since most Romans had abandoned coinage and reverted to pure barter long before the third-century crisis began in earnest
Roman silver content actually increased throughout the third century, with Gallienus's coins containing more precious metal than those of Augustus a few centuries earlier
questions.context: Diocletian's edict survives in fragments at multiple inscription sites across the Eastern empire. The pattern of currency debasement followed by price controls followed by shortages recurs across history as a unit. Bastiat's seen-and-unseen method explains it cleanly.

questions.question: At the 1922 Genoa Conference, the war-weakened European powers adopted a 'gold-exchange standard' rather than the classical gold standard. Central banks could hold reserves in dollar or sterling claims (interest-bearing) instead of physical gold. The dollar and sterling were redeemable in gold, but most reserves never circulated as metal. Why did Murray Rothbard later call this the 'inflationary' standard?
questions.answer: Reserves were claims on gold rather than gold itself, allowing the same gold to back multiple national currencies through layered claims, which expanded the global money supply
choices: Reserves were claims on gold rather than gold itself, allowing the same gold to back multiple national currencies through layered claims, which expanded the global money supply
The Genoa standard required full physical-gold backing for every banknote issued, with no claims permitted, making it more restrictive than the classical pre-1914 system
The Genoa Conference produced no actual agreement and the gold-exchange standard never came into formal effect anywhere in Europe during the entire interwar period
The Genoa standard required all currencies to be redeemable directly in silver rather than gold, and was unrelated to monetary expansion in the years leading to 1929
questions.context: Rothbard's America's Great Depression (1963) attributes much of the 1920s credit expansion to the inflationary structure of Genoa. The 1925 British return to gold at the pre-war parity (recommended by Churchill against Keynes's objections) was a parallel mistake.

questions.question: After Nixon closed the gold window on August 15, 1971, gold rose from $35/oz to over $800/oz by January 1980. Inflation hit 13.5% in 1980. Treasury yields exceeded 15%. Volcker's Federal Reserve broke the inflation by raising the fed funds rate to over 20% in June 1981, triggering a sharp recession. What does the 1970s gold-dollar dynamic show?
questions.answer: Once gold convertibility is abandoned, the only restraint on dollar depreciation is the central bank's willingness to cause politically painful recessions to defend purchasing power
choices: Once gold convertibility is abandoned, the only restraint on dollar depreciation is the central bank's willingness to cause politically painful recessions to defend purchasing power
Gold and the dollar move independently with no relationship between gold's price and the dollar's purchasing power, so the 1970s record reveals nothing about monetary regimes
The 1970s inflation was caused entirely by OPEC oil pricing decisions with no monetary contribution from the Federal Reserve or from the closure of the gold window in August 1971
Volcker's rate increases had no effect on inflation and the price level stabilized in the early 1980s due entirely to changes in OPEC pricing strategy unrelated to monetary policy
questions.context: Volcker's nomination by Carter in 1979 and his disinflation program is one of the rare cases where a central banker accepted political costs to restore monetary credibility. Reagan kept Volcker through 1987. The episode is often cited (Krugman, Friedman, Austrians) as proof that broken-money regimes are politically reversible only at high cost.

questions.question: Reagan established a Gold Commission in 1981 to study whether the United States should return to a gold standard. Ron Paul and economist Anna Schwartz served on the commission. The majority report rejected gold; Ron Paul and Lewis Lehrman filed a dissent that became a book: The Case for Gold (1982). What did the dissenters argue?
questions.answer: A gold standard would discipline the federal government's fiscal and monetary expansion, restoring the savers-protecting properties the dollar had before 1971
choices: A gold standard would discipline the federal government's fiscal and monetary expansion, restoring the savers-protecting properties the dollar had before 1971
Gold-backed currency was technically impossible to implement in modern industrial economies because there was insufficient physical gold worldwide to back the US monetary base
Returning to gold would give too much power to gold-mining nations like South Africa and the USSR, making sound-money advocates support fiat currency reluctantly
The Bretton Woods system should be reimposed with a $35/oz gold price for foreign central banks only, with no monetary effects for domestic US dollar holders or any change
questions.context: The Case for Gold (Paul + Lehrman 1982) remains a canonical popular reference. Ron Paul founded the Mises Institute board and ran for President multiple times on a gold-standard platform. The 1980s saw the end of the rapid-debasement era; the long run since has been a slower debasement.

questions.question: In November 2014, Swiss voters held a referendum on the 'Save Our Swiss Gold' initiative, which would have required the Swiss National Bank to hold 20% of reserves in physical gold within Switzerland, ban any future gold sales, and repatriate gold held abroad. The referendum failed with 77% voting NO. What was the SNB's main argument against?
questions.answer: A binding gold reserve requirement would constrain monetary policy, particularly the SNB's then-active intervention to cap the Swiss franc against the euro
choices: A binding gold reserve requirement would constrain monetary policy, particularly the SNB's then-active intervention to cap the Swiss franc against the euro
Switzerland had no gold reserves at all in 2014 and the referendum would have required the central bank to purchase gold for the first time in Swiss monetary history
Gold reserves are environmentally damaging to store, and the SNB argued the referendum would create unacceptable carbon emissions through warehouse air conditioning
The referendum would have required Switzerland to leave the European Union, which the SNB opposed even though Switzerland was not actually a member of the EU at all
questions.context: The SNB famously abandoned its euro-cap on January 15, 2015 (the 'Frankenshock'), about six weeks after the gold referendum failed. The constraint that the referendum would have imposed was exactly the kind of constraint sound-money advocates favored.

questions.question: Lyn Alden's Broken Money (2023) traces the history of money as a record-keeping technology, arguing that whenever ledger speed exceeded settlement speed, the more powerful actor captured the difference. Telegraphy in the 19th century separated the speed of payment messages from the speed of physical gold settlement, advantaging issuers. What does Alden argue about Bitcoin?
questions.answer: Bitcoin reunifies the ledger and settlement layers in software, restoring the speed-parity that broke when communications outran transport in the 19th century
choices: Bitcoin reunifies the ledger and settlement layers in software, restoring the speed-parity that broke when communications outran transport in the 19th century
Bitcoin is identical in monetary function to a standard fiat currency and offers no improvement over central-bank money in terms of payment speed or settlement properties
Bitcoin is too slow as a payment system to be useful for any practical monetary purpose and Alden argues it will be replaced by faster proof-of-stake alternatives soon
Alden argues Bitcoin is purely speculative with no monetary properties, and her book recommends gold rather than Bitcoin as the only legitimate alternative to fiat currency systems
questions.context: Alden's macroeconomic newsletter is widely read across the sound-money community. Her synthesis of monetary history and Bitcoin technical architecture is one of the most accessible adult-level treatments. The book has been translated into multiple languages.

questions.question: On September 7, 2021, El Salvador under President Nayib Bukele became the first nation to adopt Bitcoin as legal tender alongside the US dollar. The Chivo wallet was distributed to citizens with a $30 Bitcoin signup bonus. Critics including the IMF warned of financial-stability risks. By 2024, El Salvador held Bitcoin in its treasury and the homicide rate had fallen dramatically. What was Bukele's primary stated motivation?
questions.answer: Reduce remittance costs (about 24% of Salvadoran GDP), unbank the unbanked, and signal independence from the dollar system and from the IMF's monetary conditionality
choices: Reduce remittance costs (about 24% of Salvadoran GDP), unbank the unbanked, and signal independence from the dollar system and from the IMF's monetary conditionality
Replace the US dollar with Bitcoin entirely and force all Salvadorans to use Bitcoin for daily transactions, with the dollar being banned outright by the end of the year
Implement a central bank digital currency under the name 'Bitcoin' that would actually be a state-controlled token with full surveillance over every Salvadoran transaction
Comply with an IMF directive requiring El Salvador to adopt Bitcoin as part of a structural-adjustment program agreed before the September 2021 legal-tender announcement
questions.context: Remittances make up about a quarter of El Salvador's GDP. Western Union and MoneyGram historically captured 5-10% of these flows. Bukele's high domestic approval (consistently above 80%) made the gamble politically possible.

questions.question: Beginning August 2020, MicroStrategy under CEO Michael Saylor converted the bulk of its corporate treasury from US dollars into Bitcoin. The reasoning: dollar purchasing power was visibly eroding through QE and fiscal expansion. By 2024 MicroStrategy held over 200,000 BTC. The stock outperformed Bitcoin itself due to leverage and accretion. What does the Saylor playbook demonstrate?
questions.answer: A public company can adopt Bitcoin as treasury reserve to preserve purchasing power against measured dollar debasement, creating a new corporate-finance template
choices: A public company can adopt Bitcoin as treasury reserve to preserve purchasing power against measured dollar debasement, creating a new corporate-finance template
Public companies are legally required to hold their treasuries in US Treasury bills and Saylor's strategy was eventually struck down by the SEC for that reason in 2022
Saylor's strategy was abandoned in 2022 after the Bitcoin price decline and MicroStrategy reverted to holding cash in dollars by the end of the same calendar year
Bitcoin treasury strategies are restricted to private companies only and Saylor took MicroStrategy private in 2021 to implement the strategy outside public-disclosure requirements
questions.context: Saylor's argument: at zero or near-zero real rates, holding cash means accepting purchasing-power loss. Treasury rules allow non-cash reserves; Bitcoin is the hardest available reserve. The playbook has been copied by other public companies (Block, Tesla briefly, Marathon Digital, etc.).

questions.question: The cypherpunk mailing list (Eric Hughes, Tim May, John Gilmore — founded 1992) was the seedbed for Bitcoin. Adam Back's Hashcash (1997) introduced proof-of-work for anti-spam. Wei Dai's b-money proposal (1998) sketched anonymous cash. Nick Szabo's bit gold (2005) proposed unforgeable costliness. Hal Finney's RPOW (2004) explored reusable proof-of-work tokens. What did Satoshi 2008 contribute that none of the prior attempts had?
questions.answer: A working solution to the Byzantine Generals Problem for distributed money, combining proof-of-work, a public ledger, and difficulty adjustment so no central issuer was needed
choices: A working solution to the Byzantine Generals Problem for distributed money, combining proof-of-work, a public ledger, and difficulty adjustment so no central issuer was needed
A new cryptographic hash function unknown to prior cypherpunks, which solved the double-spend problem through pure mathematics alone with no network coordination
Government approval from the US Treasury, since Satoshi obtained an official Federal Reserve license before publishing the Bitcoin white paper on Halloween 2008 publicly
A team of identified developers including Adam Back, Wei Dai, and Nick Szabo who jointly authored the paper under the shared pseudonym Nakamoto for legal-protection reasons
questions.context: Hal Finney was the first recipient of Bitcoin (block 170, January 12, 2009). The cypherpunk-to-Bitcoin lineage is traced in Adam Back, Nick Szabo, and David Chaum interviews. Satoshi's identity remains unknown; the work stands.

questions.question: In February 2014 Tokyo-based Mt. Gox, then handling about 70% of global Bitcoin trading volume, filed for bankruptcy after losing about 850,000 BTC (around 7% of all bitcoin in existence at the time) to undetected theft over years. The collapse drove Bitcoin from over $1,000 to under $300. CEO Mark Karpeles faced criminal charges. What is the canonical lesson of Mt. Gox?
questions.answer: 'Not your keys, not your coins', the Bitcoin community phrase for the principle that exchange-held bitcoin is custodial credit, not actual bitcoin ownership by the depositor
choices: 'Not your keys, not your coins', the Bitcoin community phrase for the principle that exchange-held bitcoin is custodial credit, not actual bitcoin ownership by the depositor
Bitcoin is fundamentally unsafe and the entire cryptocurrency category should be abandoned, since Mt. Gox proved digital assets cannot be securely stored under any conditions
Mt. Gox proved Bitcoin should be regulated by central banks, and the case is cited by Federal Reserve officials as justification for creating a US central bank digital currency
Mt. Gox was actually a successful business that closed for unrelated reasons, with the missing 850,000 BTC being a clerical error rather than a security breach in customer accounts
questions.context: Mt. Gox stood for 'Magic: The Gathering Online Exchange', the site's original purpose before pivoting to Bitcoin. Karpeles was convicted on data-manipulation charges but acquitted on the embezzlement count. Trustee creditor distributions began 2024, a decade later.

questions.question: In May 2022 the Terra/Luna ecosystem (founder Do Kwon, Terraform Labs) collapsed. The algorithmic stablecoin UST lost its dollar peg; the Anchor protocol's 19.5% yield on UST was revealed as a subsidized loss-leader; about $60 billion in nominal value evaporated in days. Do Kwon was arrested in Montenegro in 2023. What does Terra/Luna illustrate that Bitcoin does not have?
questions.answer: An algorithmic mechanism creating value out of nothing eventually fails when the assumption it relies on (continuous inflows) ends, whereas Bitcoin has a fixed schedule and no central issuer
choices: An algorithmic mechanism creating value out of nothing eventually fails when the assumption it relies on (continuous inflows) ends, whereas Bitcoin has a fixed schedule and no central issuer
Terra/Luna and Bitcoin are functionally identical, so investors who lost money on Luna should also expect Bitcoin to collapse to zero through the same mechanism described above
Terra/Luna failed because of regulatory action by the US Treasury, and Bitcoin will eventually fail the same way through enforcement rather than any structural design flaw
Terra/Luna succeeded and is still operational, with the May 2022 events being a media-manufactured panic rather than a real economic collapse of the UST stablecoin token
questions.context: Do Kwon's later pump-and-dump prosecution (US and South Korea) is among the largest crypto-fraud cases ever brought. The episode is the canonical example of why Bitcoin advocates distinguish 'Bitcoin' from 'crypto' as different categories with different risk profiles entirely.

questions.question: The Roman aureus, gold equivalent to the silver denarius, held its metallic content far better than the denarius across the imperial period. Silver coinage debased from ~95% to under 5% between Augustus and Gallienus; the gold aureus stayed close to its weight through most of that era. Why might gold resist debasement better than silver in a long-running political order?
questions.answer: Gold coins circulated mainly among elites for large transactions where weighing caught debasement at once; silver was daily-trade money and could be diluted without immediate detection
choices: Gold coins circulated mainly among elites for large transactions where weighing caught debasement at once; silver was daily-trade money and could be diluted without immediate detection
Roman emperors imposed strict legal penalties on anyone proposing to debase the aureus but were indifferent to the silver coinage, on personal religious preferences for gold over silver
Gold is harder to melt than silver, so Roman mints lacked the technical capacity to debase the aureus and were forced to keep it at high purity throughout the imperial period
Roman silver mines exhausted in the second century AD forcing silver dilution but Roman gold mines remained productive, an entirely supply-side explanation with no monetary content
questions.context: Diocletian's currency reform around 301 AD introduced the solidus, a new gold coin that held its value through the Byzantine period (continuing as the 'bezant' for nearly a millennium). The gold solidus is among the longest-lived stable currencies in history.

questions.question: Yugoslavia's 1993-94 hyperinflation produced the highest monthly inflation rate ever measured in a country with an existing statistical system: about 313 million percent month-on-month in January 1994. The dinar was redenominated several times. Workers ran from payroll desks to shops. The breakup wars, sanctions, and the central bank's printing all fed the spiral. What stabilized it?
questions.answer: A new Super Dinar tied to the German mark at a fixed rate (January 24, 1994), accompanied by the political decision to stop the printing presses funding war and patronage
choices: A new Super Dinar tied to the German mark at a fixed rate (January 24, 1994), accompanied by the political decision to stop the printing presses funding war and patronage
Direct IMF intervention with structural-adjustment loans that retired the dinar in exchange for a new currency designed entirely by IMF staff in Washington under Bretton Woods rules
Adoption of the US dollar as Yugoslavia's sole legal tender in 1994, with the dinar formally abolished and all Yugoslav transactions denominated in dollars by federal decree
Counterfeiting by NATO intelligence services suddenly stopped after the Dayton Accords in 1995, ending the inflation without any monetary policy decision by the Yugoslav central bank
questions.context: Steve Hanke and Charles Bushnell's hyperinflation table (Cato 2017) catalogs all the worst cases historically; Yugoslavia 1994 ranks behind Hungary 1946 and Zimbabwe 2008 in headline rate but is the worst recorded outside total war or postwar occupation.

questions.question: In 1991 Argentina's economy minister Domingo Cavallo introduced the Convertibility Law, fixing the peso to the US dollar at one-to-one, with full dollar backing of the monetary base. Hyperinflation that had reached 5,000% in 1989 collapsed to near zero. The peg held for a decade. It broke catastrophically in 2001-02 in a banking and sovereign-debt crisis. Why did the peg break?
questions.answer: Fiscal deficits and provincial spending continued unchecked, so the peg eventually required defending an overvalued peso against capital flight that exceeded reserves
choices: Fiscal deficits and provincial spending continued unchecked, so the peg eventually required defending an overvalued peso against capital flight that exceeded reserves
The convertibility law was secretly abolished in 1993 by Cavallo and Argentina spent the rest of the decade pretending to maintain a peg that no longer existed officially
The 2001 collapse was caused by speculation by London-based traders alone, with no contribution from Argentine fiscal policy or from any internal financial-system factors at all
Cavallo deliberately broke the peg to enrich himself through advance knowledge of the devaluation and there were no underlying macroeconomic causes of the crisis whatsoever
questions.context: Cavallo, an Austrian-school-influenced economist, designed convertibility as a credibility device to break the printing habit. The 2001-02 crisis (corralito deposit freeze, four presidents in two weeks, partial default on $93B) ended the experiment. The mechanism itself worked while political discipline held.

questions.question: Greece joined the euro in 2001 with the help of accounting tricks (Goldman Sachs currency swaps) hiding fiscal deficits. The 2010 crisis exposed the underlying insolvency. Greece received three bailout programs (2010, 2012, 2015) totaling ~286 billion euros, conditional on austerity. The 2015 referendum rejected the conditions, but Tsipras's Syriza government accepted them anyway. Why couldn't Greece leave the euro?
questions.answer: The political and banking-system risks of a forced 'Grexit' (bank runs, capital flight, debt redenomination disputes) were judged worse than continued austerity, despite the no vote
choices: The political and banking-system risks of a forced 'Grexit' (bank runs, capital flight, debt redenomination disputes) were judged worse than continued austerity, despite the no vote
Greece was legally prohibited from leaving the euro by EU treaty provisions and any attempt would have automatically expelled Greece from NATO and the United Nations simultaneously
The Greek drachma had been physically destroyed during the 2001 conversion and there was no technical way to reissue it within the timeframe the political crisis required
Greek public opinion strongly opposed leaving the euro across all party lines, with no significant political faction supporting return to the drachma during the entire crisis period
questions.context: Mario Draghi's July 2012 'whatever it takes' commitment to defend the euro is the canonical central-banker rhetorical intervention of the decade. Greek GDP fell about 25% peak-to-trough during the crisis. Unemployment exceeded 27%. The deeper question (whether eurozone-without-fiscal-union was ever sustainable) remains open.

questions.question: On the Pacific island of Yap, large stone disks called 'rai' have served as a form of money for centuries. The stones, some weighing several tons, are too heavy to move; ownership transfers verbally with community memory recording who owns which stone. One famous stone reportedly sat at the bottom of the sea after a transport accident yet continued to circulate as currency. Friedman wrote about Yap in 1991. What does the Yap system illustrate?
questions.answer: Money is fundamentally a shared ledger rather than a physical object; the stones are simply a memorable, hard-to-forge accounting unit that the community tracks together
choices: Money is fundamentally a shared ledger rather than a physical object; the stones are simply a memorable, hard-to-forge accounting unit that the community tracks together
Money must be physically present to function, and the Yap system actually collapsed in the 19th century when European traders demanded physical possession of stones for any payment
The Yap stones were used only ceremonially and never functioned as actual money in the sense of being exchanged for goods or services in any practical Yap commerce
Money requires central-bank issuance to be valid, and the Yap stones were issued by a small council of elders that functioned identically to a modern central bank with full powers
questions.context: Friedman's essay 'The Island of Stone Money' (1991) is the canonical economist treatment. The Yap system has been cited by Bitcoin proponents (the chain is the shared ledger) and by sovereign-money critics (proof that money is a social institution, not an inherent property of objects).

questions.question: China has worked since the 2000s to internationalize the renminbi (RMB) as a partial alternative to the US dollar. The 2016 IMF SDR-basket inclusion (the RMB joined at 10.92% weight) was a milestone. By 2024 the RMB was still under 5% of global reserves and well under 5% of global trade settlement, despite China being the world's largest exporter. Why hasn't the RMB displaced the dollar?
questions.answer: Reserve-currency status requires open capital accounts, trusted property rights, and credible legal recourse, none of which China extends to foreign holders of RMB at the scale of the dollar
choices: Reserve-currency status requires open capital accounts, trusted property rights, and credible legal recourse, none of which China extends to foreign holders of RMB at the scale of the dollar
The Chinese government doesn't want the RMB to be a reserve currency and has actively blocked its use abroad since at least 2010 to keep the dollar dominant for geopolitical reasons
The RMB has already largely replaced the dollar in global trade by 2024, with most international transactions now denominated in RMB rather than US dollars worldwide currently
The RMB and the dollar are functionally identical and statistical measures showing dollar dominance are misleading, since most reserves are actually held in mixed dollar-RMB synthetic instruments
questions.context: Reserve-currency status requires the issuer to run persistent current-account deficits to supply the world with the currency (Triffin dilemma). China's export-driven model makes this politically difficult. Capital-account closure during stress (2015-16 Shanghai event) further undermined trust.

questions.question: In 1896 William Jennings Bryan delivered his 'Cross of Gold' speech at the Democratic Convention, demanding the US monetize silver at a 16:1 ratio with gold. The post-1873 demonetization of silver (the 'Crime of '73') had contracted the money supply during a deflationary era. Farmers and debtors favored bimetallism; eastern creditors favored gold. McKinley won the election. What was at stake economically?
questions.answer: Bimetallism would have expanded the money supply, helping debtors at the expense of creditors; the choice was a distributional one masked as a monetary one
choices: Bimetallism would have expanded the money supply, helping debtors at the expense of creditors; the choice was a distributional one masked as a monetary one
Bimetallism was technically impossible to implement in a 19th-century industrial economy because chemical assaying could not reliably distinguish gold from silver at the necessary accuracy
Free silver had no economic content and was purely a rhetorical issue with no measurable consequences for the US money supply or for the relative position of any economic class

Bryan's free-silver platform was actually supported by all eastern banks and the gold-standard victory in 1896 represented a populist movement against entrenched financial interests rather than the reverse
questions.context: L. Frank Baum's The Wonderful Wizard of Oz (1900) has been read by some scholars (Hugh Rockoff 1990) as a monetary allegory — yellow brick road (gold), silver slippers, Dorothy from Kansas (the populist farm-belt voter). The allegorical reading is contested; the political moment is not.

questions.question: The Bank for International Settlements (BIS), founded in 1930 in Basel, Switzerland, is the central bank of central banks. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (founded 1974) sets capital and liquidity standards: Basel I (1988), Basel II (2004), Basel III (2010), Basel III Endgame (negotiated 2020s). What is the structural concern about Basel rules from a sound-money perspective?
questions.answer: Basel standards treat sovereign debt as 'risk-free' for capital purposes, channeling bank lending toward government rather than productive uses and entrenching the central-bank/Treasury nexus
choices: Basel standards treat sovereign debt as 'risk-free' for capital purposes, channeling bank lending toward government rather than productive uses and entrenching the central-bank/Treasury nexus
Basel standards are designed to maximize free-market competition among banks, with no preferential treatment of sovereign debt or any other asset class in the capital framework
Basel standards are voluntary and have no measurable effect on bank behavior anywhere in the world, so the question of sovereign-debt treatment in the framework is academic only
Basel standards penalize sovereign-debt holdings heavily, requiring banks to hold extra capital against any government bond purchases, which makes them strongly anti-government in design
questions.context: The 'sovereign-debt is risk-free' assumption in Basel rules has been criticized by Austrian, post-Keynesian, and mainstream observers (Reinhart-Rogoff). The euro-area crisis (Greece, Portugal, Italy bonds held by their own banks) revealed the assumption's danger.

questions.question: In January 2023, developer Casey Rodarmor introduced 'Ordinals', a protocol that allows arbitrary data (images, text, even small applications) to be inscribed on individual satoshis. Bitcoin fees spiked. The community split: some saw 'inscriptions' as a fee market boon, others as bloat threatening Bitcoin's monetary purpose. What does the controversy illustrate about Bitcoin governance?
questions.answer: Bitcoin has no central authority to ban a use case once it is technically possible; the community debates and the market decides through fee-rate competition for block space
choices: Bitcoin has no central authority to ban a use case once it is technically possible; the community debates and the market decides through fee-rate competition for block space
The Bitcoin Foundation banned Ordinals in February 2023 and developers who continued to support them were expelled from the open-source repository under formal disciplinary procedures
The Federal Reserve approved Ordinals as part of its CBDC interoperability framework, and Bitcoin Core developers implemented the changes at the request of the US Treasury directly
Ordinals was a brief experiment that was abandoned in 2023 with no lasting effect on Bitcoin transaction volumes or on fee dynamics in any subsequent halving cycle on the network
questions.context: The Ordinals debate is a contemporary example of Bitcoin's permissionless-innovation property AND its open-governance challenges. Block-space scarcity disciplines the market; the protocol allows what the protocol allows. The episode also drove fee revenue to miners, helping Bitcoin's long-run security budget.

questions.question: The Lightning Network, proposed by Joseph Poon and Thaddeus Dryja in 2015 and live since 2018, is a Bitcoin layer-2 payment system. Users open payment channels with locked Bitcoin, transact instantly off-chain, and settle on the main chain when channels close. Lightning supports millions of transactions per second in theory. Why is Lightning seen as essential to Bitcoin's monetary use case?
questions.answer: Bitcoin's base layer settles roughly 7 transactions per second to maintain decentralization; Lightning scales payments without compromising the base layer's monetary properties
choices: Bitcoin's base layer settles roughly 7 transactions per second to maintain decentralization; Lightning scales payments without compromising the base layer's monetary properties
Lightning replaces Bitcoin entirely with a new proof-of-stake consensus mechanism and is intended to make the original Bitcoin protocol obsolete by the end of the decade
Lightning is operated by a centralized company in Switzerland that holds custody of all funds in payment channels, similar to traditional payment processors like Visa and Mastercard
Lightning was abandoned in 2020 after failing to attract significant user adoption and is no longer an active part of the Bitcoin ecosystem despite occasional references in technical papers
questions.context: Lightning capacity grew from ~100 BTC in 2019 to over 5,000 BTC by 2024. El Salvador's Chivo wallet uses Lightning for daily transactions. The Cash App and Strike integrations brought Lightning to mainstream US users. The 'scaling debate' of 2015-17 (Bitcoin Cash hard fork) was effectively settled by Lightning's success.

questions.question: Bitcoin's 'block size war' of 2015-2017 pitted larger-block advocates (Bitcoin Cash, Bitcoin Unlimited) against off-chain scalers via Segregated Witness (SegWit) and Lightning. August 2017 SegWit activated via miner signaling without a hard fork. The November 2017 'Segwit2X' attempt to force a 2MB hard fork was abandoned. What was the disagreement?
questions.answer: Whether to scale Bitcoin by raising on-chain capacity (sacrificing some decentralization) or by building payment layers on top while keeping the base layer small and verifiable
choices: Whether to scale Bitcoin by raising on-chain capacity (sacrificing some decentralization) or by building payment layers on top while keeping the base layer small and verifiable
Whether Bitcoin should adopt the Ethereum smart-contract framework as its primary use case or remain limited to simple monetary transfers as Satoshi originally intended in 2008
Whether Bitcoin should transition to proof-of-stake consensus or remain on proof-of-work, with the small-block faction representing proof-of-stake advocates against the larger group
Whether Bitcoin should be administered by a central foundation or remain decentralized, with the large-block faction supporting a new Bitcoin Foundation board to govern protocol
questions.context: Roger Ver, Jihan Wu, and others led the Bitcoin Cash fork in August 2017. By 2024, BCH had a tiny fraction of Bitcoin's market cap and adoption. The small-block side's bet on Lightning + base-layer decentralization is now considered vindicated by market action.

questions.question: The Aldrich Plan drafted at Jekyll Island in November 1910 by Senator Nelson Aldrich and Wall Street bankers was rejected by Congress in 1912 as too obviously a banker-run scheme. Carter Glass and Robert Owen modified it: same regional-reserve-bank architecture, with a federal Board of Governors overlaid for political cover. The Federal Reserve Act passed December 23, 1913. What changed substantively?
questions.answer: Glass-Owen kept the Aldrich Plan's bank-friendly regional structure and added a thin layer of presidential appointment, so the underlying private-bank coordination survived intact
choices: Glass-Owen kept the Aldrich Plan's bank-friendly regional structure and added a thin layer of presidential appointment, so the underlying private-bank coordination survived intact
Glass-Owen eliminated all private-bank involvement in the Federal Reserve System, making the Fed a fully public agency under direct Treasury Department control from 1913 onward
The Aldrich Plan and Glass-Owen were completely different proposals with no architectural similarity, and the eventual Federal Reserve owed nothing to the Jekyll Island meeting
The Aldrich Plan was adopted unchanged in 1913 and Glass-Owen was a separate piece of banking legislation passed in 1933 unrelated to the original Federal Reserve creation at all
questions.context: Aldrich was Rockefeller's father-in-law. Paul Warburg (Kuhn Loeb) drafted much of the technical detail. Wilson signed the act two days before Christmas with most of Congress already departed.

questions.question: Benjamin Strong was governor of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York from 1914 until his death in 1928. Strong dominated Fed policy through informal channels with British central banker Montagu Norman, coordinating to keep US rates low so European countries could rebuild gold reserves after WWI. Rothbard's America's Great Depression (1963) blamed Strong for fueling the 1920s credit boom. What did Strong's coordination produce?
questions.answer: Easy-money credit expansion in the late 1920s that inflated stocks and housing, setting up the boom that crashed in 1929 and the depression that followed for a decade
choices: Easy-money credit expansion in the late 1920s that inflated stocks and housing, setting up the boom that crashed in 1929 and the depression that followed for a decade
Tight-money discipline that kept the US economy growing steadily throughout the 1920s with no measurable contribution to the 1929 crash or any subsequent economic difficulties
Strong's policies had no measurable effect on US economic activity in the 1920s and the 1929 crash was caused entirely by speculation by individual investors without monetary causes
A balanced policy combining tight and easy money in alternating cycles that produced stable growth and was widely admired by Strong's successors throughout the rest of the 20th century
questions.context: Strong's death in October 1928 left the Fed leaderless during the critical 1929-33 period. The internal Fed disputes (NY vs Washington, real-bills vs free-market) over how to respond to the crash contributed to the policy paralysis Friedman + Schwartz later blamed for the depression's depth.

questions.question: Between 1929 and 1933, the US money supply (M1) fell by about one-third. Roughly 9,000 banks failed; depositors lost about $7 billion in savings. The Federal Reserve, with the legal authority to act as lender of last resort, did not. Friedman and Schwartz's 1963 A Monetary History argued this was the Fed's central failure. What policy choice produced the contraction?
questions.answer: The Fed allowed bank failures to cascade by refusing to provide adequate emergency liquidity, on the 'real bills doctrine' view that liquidating bad banks was healthy
choices: The Fed allowed bank failures to cascade by refusing to provide adequate emergency liquidity, on the 'real bills doctrine' view that liquidating bad banks was healthy
The Fed aggressively expanded the money supply in 1929-33 but the contraction happened anyway due to private-sector deleveraging that the central bank could not influence
The Fed was legally prohibited from intervening before the Glass-Steagall Act of 1933 and had no tools available to provide liquidity to failing banks during the entire period
The Fed actively printed money to cause the contraction as part of a deliberate political conspiracy to harm small banks and consolidate banking power among the large New York institutions
questions.context: Bernanke's 2002 'I'd like to say to Milton and Anna: we did it, we're very sorry, but we won't do it again' speech (Friedman's 90th birthday) was the Fed's formal acknowledgment of the 1929-33 failure. Whether the post-2008 response actually avoided the mistake or repeated it in different form is contested.

questions.question: Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz published A Monetary History of the United States 1867-1960 in 1963 after about 15 years of research at NBER. The 860-page work changed how the Great Depression is taught. Their core thesis: the Depression was not an inevitable consequence of 1920s excesses, but a Fed policy failure. What is the broader recognition that follows from their argument?
questions.answer: Central-bank decisions can turn ordinary recessions into depressions, so the institutional design of the Fed deserves as much scrutiny as the business cycles it claims to manage
choices: Central-bank decisions can turn ordinary recessions into depressions, so the institutional design of the Fed deserves as much scrutiny as the business cycles it claims to manage
Central-bank decisions have no measurable effect on aggregate economic activity, so the Friedman-Schwartz volume is interesting history but provides no policy lessons for any modern central bank
Central banks are necessary because Friedman-Schwartz proved no economy can function without one, and the volume is the canonical reference for modern central-bank-supremacy arguments
Friedman and Schwartz were Marxist economists whose volume argued for the abolition of capitalism, and their work has been used to justify centrally planned economies in postwar Europe and Asia
questions.context: Anna Schwartz was the unsung hand on the research side; Friedman supplied the public-intellectual presence. The volume's documentary discipline (every claim sourced to Fed records, Treasury reports, contemporary newspapers) remains a model for the genre.

questions.question: Paul Volcker, nominated by Carter in August 1979 and reappointed by Reagan in 1983, raised the federal funds rate to over 20% by June 1981 to break the entrenched inflation of the 1970s. Unemployment rose to 10.8% in 1982. Farmers drove tractors to the Fed building in Washington in protest. CPI inflation fell from 13.5% (1980) to 3.2% (1983). What did Volcker demonstrate?
questions.answer: Persistent inflation can be broken by a central bank willing to cause politically painful recessions to restore monetary credibility, but only if the political will exists to absorb the cost
choices: Persistent inflation can be broken by a central bank willing to cause politically painful recessions to restore monetary credibility, but only if the political will exists to absorb the cost
Inflation always falls naturally without any central-bank action, and the 1980s decline in CPI was caused entirely by changes in OPEC oil pricing strategy with no monetary contribution
High interest rates have no effect on inflation, and the Volcker disinflation was actually a coincidence with the natural end of the 1970s inflationary spiral through other unrelated mechanisms
Volcker actually cut interest rates in 1981 and the inflation decline was caused by the rate cuts rather than by the much smaller earlier increases that were politically symbolic only
questions.context: Volcker's willingness to break inflation at high political cost is the canonical counterexample to public-choice predictions that central bankers will always inflate. The discipline did not survive: post-Volcker Fed chairs have presided over expanding balance sheets and serial bailouts.

questions.question: Beginning with the October 19, 1987 Black Monday crash, Alan Greenspan's Federal Reserve repeatedly cut rates to support falling asset markets: 1987 crash, 1998 LTCM/Russia, 2001 dot-com crash, 2003 jobless recovery. Markets came to expect a 'Greenspan put' — central-bank rate cuts cushioning every selloff. What economic distortion does this create?
questions.answer: Moral hazard, in which investors take excessive risks knowing the Fed will socialize losses by cutting rates whenever asset markets decline, encouraging more risk-taking
choices: Moral hazard, in which investors take excessive risks knowing the Fed will socialize losses by cutting rates whenever asset markets decline, encouraging more risk-taking
No distortion, since the Fed's intervention restores normal market function and there is no measurable change in risk-taking behavior by investors as a result of expected rate cuts
A negative distortion, since investors actually reduce risk-taking when they expect Fed intervention, leading to under-investment in productive enterprises across the economy
The Greenspan put is a media fiction with no basis in actual Fed policy, and rate cuts during the 1987-2008 period were entirely uncorrelated with any movements in asset markets
questions.context: The 'Bernanke put' and 'Yellen put' and 'Powell put' continued the pattern under successive Fed chairs. The 2008 GFC is often interpreted as the bill coming due on a generation of moral-hazard-encouraged risk-taking; the 2020 pandemic response massively expanded the underlying habit.

questions.question: On March 14, 2008, the Federal Reserve provided emergency funding to JP Morgan Chase to acquire failing investment bank Bear Stearns for $2 per share (later raised to $10). The Fed guaranteed about $30 billion of Bear's distressed assets through a special-purpose vehicle (Maiden Lane). The action used Section 13(3) emergency powers not used since the 1930s. What precedent did this set?
questions.answer: The Fed extended its lender-of-last-resort function from commercial banks to investment banks, signaling that 'too big to fail' applied to Wall Street firms outside its traditional regulatory perimeter
choices: The Fed extended its lender-of-last-resort function from commercial banks to investment banks, signaling that 'too big to fail' applied to Wall Street firms outside its traditional regulatory perimeter
The Fed declined to intervene with Bear Stearns and the firm was liquidated through ordinary bankruptcy proceedings with no use of emergency lending authority by any federal agency
The Fed nationalized Bear Stearns under direct federal ownership, and the firm continued to operate as a government-owned investment bank until being sold back to private investors in 2015
The Fed's intervention was authorized by Congress through a specific statute passed in March 2008 just before the Bear Stearns rescue, and was not based on any pre-existing emergency authority
questions.context: The Lehman decision six months later (Sept 15, 2008 — let Lehman fail) puzzled the market: why was Bear saved and Lehman not? Bernanke's later explanation pointed to legal technicalities (collateral inadequacy) but the inconsistency rattled the system.

questions.question: On Sunday September 14, 2008, Treasury Secretary Hank Paulson and Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke met with Wall Street CEOs at the NY Fed. They declined to backstop Lehman Brothers. Lehman filed for bankruptcy at 1:45am Monday September 15 — the largest bankruptcy in US history at $639 billion in assets. The next day AIG received an $85 billion Fed bridge loan. What did the contrast reveal?
questions.answer: The selective bailout decisions were political and ad-hoc, not principled, so markets read the message that Fed-Treasury support depended on connections rather than legal rules
choices: The selective bailout decisions were political and ad-hoc, not principled, so markets read the message that Fed-Treasury support depended on connections rather than legal rules
The bailout decisions were strictly rule-based, with Lehman failing automatic legal criteria for federal support and AIG meeting them through a clearly defined collateral test
Lehman was not actually allowed to fail and the firm continued operations under federal ownership until 2012, with the 2008 bankruptcy filing being a media-manufactured event
AIG was allowed to fail and ordinary bankruptcy proceedings were used, with the $85 billion figure being a media exaggeration of routine Federal Reserve liquidity operations
questions.context: Lehman CEO Dick Fuld's memoir and the FCIC report (Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission 2011) document the bailout decisions. AIG's bailout ultimately reached $182 billion. About $100 billion went through AIG to Goldman Sachs and other counterparties at 100 cents on the dollar — the so-called 'backdoor bailout'.

questions.question: The Emergency Economic Stabilization Act of October 3, 2008 created TARP (Troubled Asset Relief Program), authorizing $700 billion in Treasury purchases of toxic assets and direct equity injections into banks. The vote initially failed in the House September 29 (Dow fell 778 points). It passed October 3 after sweeteners. What does TARP illustrate?
questions.answer: When a financial crisis becomes acute enough, political resistance to bailouts collapses, so 'too big to fail' effectively negates democratic constraints once contagion is feared
choices: When a financial crisis becomes acute enough, political resistance to bailouts collapses, so 'too big to fail' effectively negates democratic constraints once contagion is feared
Democratic constraints on bailouts are highly effective and TARP was actually rejected by Congress, with the $700 billion being authorized through executive action only by the Treasury
TARP was a small program with no measurable effect on the financial system, and the actual recovery from the 2008 crisis was driven entirely by private-sector deleveraging without intervention
TARP was used exclusively to purchase toxic mortgage assets at market prices and the equity injections into banks happened through a separate program with full congressional approval at each stage
