questions.context: Direct equity injections into the nine largest US banks happened October 13-14, 2008 — Paulson convened the CEOs at Treasury and informed them they would accept federal capital. Net TARP losses to taxpayers were eventually small; the precedent established was large.

questions.question: The Federal Reserve's balance sheet stood at about $870 billion in August 2007. By the end of QE3 (October 2014) it had reached about $4.5 trillion. QE1 (Nov 2008-Mar 2010): $1.25T mortgage-backed securities + $300B Treasuries. QE2 (Nov 2010-June 2011): $600B Treasuries. QE3 (Sep 2012-Oct 2014): $85B/month open-ended. What was the substantive theory underlying QE?
questions.answer: Lower long-term rates and inflated asset prices would induce wealth-effect spending and investment, even though the prior 'zero lower bound' suggested traditional monetary policy was exhausted
choices: Lower long-term rates and inflated asset prices would induce wealth-effect spending and investment, even though the prior 'zero lower bound' suggested traditional monetary policy was exhausted
QE was designed to directly inject cash into household bank accounts to stimulate consumer spending, similar to a universal basic income program implemented through the central bank
QE was a routine open-market operation with no special theoretical justification and no measurable difference from ordinary Federal Reserve policy under chairmen Greenspan or Volcker in any era
QE was a fiscal program disguised as monetary policy, with the Federal Reserve directly purchasing goods and services from US households on behalf of the federal government for several years
questions.context: The wealth-effect channel worked: asset prices recovered strongly, with the S&P 500 quadrupling from March 2009 to early 2020. The distributional consequences (Cantillon effect — gains concentrated among asset holders) are now widely acknowledged, including by Fed officials in retirement.

questions.question: Between March and December 2020 the Federal Reserve expanded its balance sheet from $4T to over $7T, cut the funds rate to 0-0.25%, and launched corporate and municipal lending. Congress passed CARES ($2.2T) and additional packages through December. Total 2020-21 fiscal response approached $5T. What concerned sound-money critics?
questions.answer: This scale of combined monetary and fiscal expansion in peacetime had no precedent and would either show up as inflation, as asset bubbles, or as both, with savers paying the bill
choices: This scale of combined monetary and fiscal expansion in peacetime had no precedent and would either show up as inflation, as asset bubbles, or as both, with savers paying the bill
The 2020 monetary and fiscal response was modest by historical standards and similar to ordinary recessionary policy used in many prior US recessions throughout the 20th century
Sound-money critics supported the 2020 response and there was no significant Austrian-school critique of the policies pursued by Powell, Mnuchin, and the congressional leadership during the year
The 2020 monetary expansion was funded entirely by foreign central banks rather than by Federal Reserve money creation, so it had no measurable effect on the US money supply during this period
questions.context: Inflation appeared in 2021 and peaked at 9.1% CPI year-on-year in June 2022. Asset prices set records through 2021. The 2022 stock market correction and 2023 banking turmoil (SVB, Signature, First Republic, Credit Suisse) were the partial bill coming due. The longer-term consequences remain to be settled.

questions.question: Stephanie Kelton's The Deficit Myth (2020) became the most popular statement of Modern Monetary Theory. Core thesis: a country issuing its own currency cannot 'run out of money' the way a household can; the only constraint on government spending is inflation, not solvency. The 2021-23 US inflation reached 9.1% (June 2022 peak). What did the real-world test reveal?
questions.answer: When the inflation constraint MMT acknowledged arrived, it arrived larger, faster, and more persistent than the framework's popular deployment suggested, falsifying MMT's permissive policy implications
choices: When the inflation constraint MMT acknowledged arrived, it arrived larger, faster, and more persistent than the framework's popular deployment suggested, falsifying MMT's permissive policy implications
MMT was vindicated since inflation returned to 3% by 2023, demonstrating that the framework provides accurate guidance for fiscal-monetary policy under any post-pandemic conditions in any country
MMT made no predictions about inflation and the 2021-23 episode has no bearing on the theory, which is purely a description of accounting identities with no empirical content of any kind
MMT was abandoned by Kelton in 2022 and the framework no longer has any active proponents in academic or policy circles, having been definitively refuted by Larry Summers in his February 2021 op-ed
questions.context: Kelton herself acknowledged the inflation constraint in her formal academic work. The political deployment of MMT systematically downplayed the constraint. The popular case for MMT aged poorly through 2021-23.

questions.question: On February 4, 2021, former Treasury Secretary Larry Summers wrote a Washington Post op-ed warning that Biden's American Rescue Plan ($1.9T on top of December 2020's $900B) was several times larger than the output gap and would cause inflation. The piece was attacked as fear-mongering. Inflation hit 9.1% by June 2022. What does Summers's warning illustrate?
questions.answer: Even a center-left economist applying basic macroeconomic arithmetic was vindicated by inflation that the policy consensus dismissed, revealing how ideologically captive the policy consensus had become
choices: Even a center-left economist applying basic macroeconomic arithmetic was vindicated by inflation that the policy consensus dismissed, revealing how ideologically captive the policy consensus had become
Summers's warning was attention-seeking and the 2021-23 inflation was caused entirely by supply-chain disruptions from COVID with no contribution from any fiscal or monetary expansion at any time

Summers retracted his warning in late 2021 after the Biden administration's fiscal advisers persuaded him the inflation forecast was wrong, with the 2022 inflation coming as a surprise to all economists
Summers's warning was correct only by chance and his methodology had no merit, since the inflation could equally have been zero given the underlying randomness of price-level dynamics in 2021
questions.context: Summers had served as Clinton's Treasury Secretary and as a senior Obama economic adviser. His vindication is awkward for both the Biden-era center-left and the academic profession that lined up against him. The mainstream's failure to model the inflation correctly is the bigger story.

questions.question: US CPI inflation peaked at 9.1% year-on-year in June 2022, the highest since November 1981. Producer prices peaked higher. The Fed had begun raising rates from 0 in March 2022; the fed funds rate reached 5.25-5.50% by July 2023. Inflation fell to ~3% by mid-2023. What was the central recognition for sound-money observers?
questions.answer: Inflation is a monetary phenomenon when the cumulative excess money creation exceeds productive capacity growth, regardless of whether mainstream macro models predict it correctly in advance
choices: Inflation is a monetary phenomenon when the cumulative excess money creation exceeds productive capacity growth, regardless of whether mainstream macro models predict it correctly in advance
Inflation has no monetary cause and the 2021-23 episode was caused entirely by Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 with no contribution from prior monetary or fiscal policy decisions
Inflation is always 2% or below in modern economies and the 2022 measurement was an aberration caused by statistical-reporting errors at the Bureau of Labor Statistics in the post-pandemic period
Inflation is irrelevant to monetary policy and the Federal Reserve's rate increases in 2022-23 were unnecessary, with the price level decline happening through unrelated supply-side factors only
questions.context: Friedman's 1963 dictum 'inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon' was widely mocked through the 2010s low-inflation era. The 2021-23 inflation made the dictum look prescient again. The mechanism (Cantillon effect, money supply transmission to asset and then consumer prices) operated roughly as Austrian theory predicts.

questions.question: John Maynard Keynes's General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money (1936) was the most influential economics book of the 20th century. Its core claim: markets do not automatically clear at full employment, and government deficit spending can lift the economy out of slumps through the multiplier effect. What is the Austrian critique of the General Theory's foundational move?
questions.answer: Keynes treated capital as a homogeneous aggregate, ignoring the structure of production (stages, durations, interest-rate sensitivity) that determines whether stimulus produces real growth or merely malinvestment
choices: Keynes treated capital as a homogeneous aggregate, ignoring the structure of production (stages, durations, interest-rate sensitivity) that determines whether stimulus produces real growth or merely malinvestment
Austrian economists agreed with the General Theory and Hayek wrote a positive review in 1936 praising Keynes's analytical framework, with the Austrian-Keynesian divide being a postwar invention
The General Theory was rejected by every contemporary economist of note in 1936 and was only rediscovered in the 1970s after a long period of complete obscurity
The General Theory is a Marxist work and the Austrian critique focused on its rejection of capitalism rather than on any specific analytical claims about employment, interest, or money
questions.context: Hayek's 1931 review of Keynes's Treatise on Money was the canonical Austrian critique of the pre-General-Theory Keynes. Hayek's failure to write a comparable response to the General Theory itself is one of the historical 'what ifs' of 20th-century economics. Rothbard, Garrison, and Hülsmann developed the response posthumously.

questions.question: Keynes's General Theory introduces 'animal spirits', the irrational psychological currents that drive entrepreneurial investment beyond rational calculation. Akerlof and Shiller revived it in their 2009 Animal Spirits. What is the Austrian objection to animal spirits as a stand-alone explanation of investment cycles?
questions.answer: Investment cycles correlate systematically with monetary policy and credit expansion; 'animal spirits' is an unfalsifiable label that conceals rather than explains the boom-bust pattern Mises and Hayek named
choices: Investment cycles correlate systematically with monetary policy and credit expansion; 'animal spirits' is an unfalsifiable label that conceals rather than explains the boom-bust pattern Mises and Hayek named

Austrians accept the animal-spirits explanation fully and the entire Austrian Business Cycle Theory is identical to Keynes's framework with different terminology applied to the same underlying psychological dynamics

Animal spirits is the central Austrian concept and was originated by Menger in 1871, with Keynes borrowing the idea without attribution in his 1936 General Theory under a slightly modified terminology

Investment cycles do not actually exist and the apparent boom-bust pattern is a statistical illusion, so the question of animal spirits versus monetary explanation has no factual content for any economist
questions.context: The Austrian objection is that 'animal spirits' is non-falsifiable: any investment decline can be attributed to psychological retreat after the fact, with no predictive content. ABCT, by contrast, predicts investment patterns based on monetary expansion below the natural interest rate. The 2008 GFC was a clean test, and Austrians won it.

questions.question: The Phillips curve, charted by A.W. Phillips in 1958, showed an inverse relationship between UK unemployment and wage growth. Samuelson and Solow translated it for US policy. The 1960s consensus held policymakers could choose a point: higher inflation for lower unemployment. The 1970s stagflation broke it. What did Friedman's 1968 lecture predict?
questions.answer: Workers and firms would build inflation expectations into wage and price decisions, shifting the curve up, so there is no stable trade-off, only a temporary one that erodes over time
choices: Workers and firms would build inflation expectations into wage and price decisions, shifting the curve up, so there is no stable trade-off, only a temporary one that erodes over time

The Phillips curve is a stable empirical regularity that has held throughout the 20th century with no breakdown, and the 1970s stagflation was a statistical artifact rather than a real economic phenomenon
The Phillips curve was vindicated by the 1970s data, with the apparent stagflation being a misreading of the relationship between wage growth and unemployment rather than a genuine model failure
Friedman supported the Phillips curve and his 1968 lecture endorsed its use for monetary policy, with the curve only being criticized by Friedman much later in his 1980s public writings on the topic
questions.context: Friedman's 'The Role of Monetary Policy' (American Economic Review 1968, presidential address) predicted the breakdown before it happened. Edmund Phelps reached similar conclusions independently. The expectations-augmented Phillips curve became the mainstream model after the 1970s; the deeper lesson — that stable monetary trade-offs are illusory — is still resisted.

questions.question: Hayek's Prices and Production (1931) is the canonical statement of the Austrian Business Cycle Theory. Hayek diagrammed the economy as stages of production, from raw materials through intermediate goods to consumer goods, each requiring time. Lowering interest rates artificially lengthens the production structure beyond what real savings support, producing malinvestment. When the boom corrects, what happens?
questions.answer: Capital tied up in unprofitable longer-stage projects must be liquidated, workers must move between sectors, and the recession is the needed correction of the prior monetary distortion
choices: Capital tied up in unprofitable longer-stage projects must be liquidated, workers must move between sectors, and the recession is the needed correction of the prior monetary distortion
Capital adjusts smoothly with no recession, since markets price information immediately and there are no real economic costs from monetary policy shifts under any circumstances at all
The central bank prevents the recession through countercyclical policy and there is no period of correction, with the boom merely transitioning into a permanent higher-growth steady state
Workers cannot move between sectors so the recession affects only specific industries, with aggregate output and employment unaffected by the monetary distortion or its eventual correction
questions.context: Hayek's Hayekian triangles diagram the production structure visually. The 1931 lectures at LSE were the moment Austrian theory entered the English-speaking academy. Hayek's 1974 Nobel cited his cycle theory specifically. The 2008 GFC's pattern (housing-construction boom from Fed easy money, then capital liquidation) matches the Hayek framework cleanly.

questions.question: Ludwig von Mises's The Theory of Money and Credit (1912) was the first systematic Austrian treatment of money. Mises extended Carl Menger's 1871 marginal-utility framework to money, solving what came to be called the 'Mises regression theorem': money's value can be traced back through time to its original commodity-money use. What problem does the regression theorem solve?
questions.answer: Why people accept money today (its prior purchasing power gives current expectations) ultimately grounding money's value in past commodity use rather than circular subjective valuation
choices: Why people accept money today (its prior purchasing power gives current expectations) ultimately grounding money's value in past commodity use rather than circular subjective valuation
Why money is necessary for economic activity at all, since the regression theorem proves that barter economies are impossible due to the double-coincidence-of-wants problem unsolvable otherwise
Why central banks should issue currency rather than private banks, since the regression theorem requires governmental backing to establish initial commodity-money status for any monetary unit
Why fiat money cannot exist according to Mises, since the regression theorem mathematically proves that all sustainable monetary systems must remain fully convertible to a specific physical commodity
questions.context: The regression theorem became controversial again with Bitcoin. Critics argued Bitcoin cannot be money because it has no prior commodity use; defenders argued Bitcoin's monetary properties (scarcity, divisibility, fungibility, durability, recognizability, portability) bootstrap its monetary status without need for a commodity origin. The debate is unresolved among Austrians.

questions.question: In 1931 Hayek wrote a critical review of Keynes's Treatise on Money in Economica. Keynes responded by reviewing Hayek's Prices and Production. Both grew frustrated with the other's failure to engage. Hayek did not write a comparable response to Keynes's General Theory (1936). Why is this absence a major regret?
questions.answer: The General Theory dominated postwar policy without facing the sustained Austrian critique Hayek had given the Treatise, so Keynesianism became consensus partly by default rather than by winning the argument
choices: The General Theory dominated postwar policy without facing the sustained Austrian critique Hayek had given the Treatise, so Keynesianism became consensus partly by default rather than by winning the argument

Hayek's 1936 review of the General Theory was the canonical Austrian response and was widely cited in subsequent economic literature, making the postwar Keynesian dominance entirely a matter of argument
The Treatise on Money was actually more influential than the General Theory and Hayek's critique of the Treatise effectively defeated Keynes's framework in the academic mainstream during the 1930s
Hayek and Keynes were close personal friends and never engaged in any public economic debate, with the 'Hayek-Keynes debate' being a postwar invention by Rothbard and his followers in the 1970s
questions.context: Hayek later said he had hesitated to respond because Keynes's framework kept shifting. He also worked on his political-philosophy book The Road to Serfdom (1944) during the war years. The Mont Pelerin Society he founded in 1947 became the institutional vehicle for the classical-liberal counter-tradition.

questions.question: Obama's $787B American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (Feb 2009) was sold on a fiscal multiplier of ~1.5: every $1 spent would produce $1.50 of GDP. The Romer-Romer projections forecast unemployment peaking under 8% with stimulus, above 9% without. Actual unemployment peaked at 10% in October 2009 with the stimulus in effect. What was the recognition?
questions.answer: The fiscal multiplier was much smaller than mainstream Keynesian models predicted, possibly below 1.0, so government spending crowded out private activity rather than adding to it on net
choices: The fiscal multiplier was much smaller than mainstream Keynesian models predicted, possibly below 1.0, so government spending crowded out private activity rather than adding to it on net

The fiscal multiplier was higher than predicted at over 3.0, with the actual outcome being vastly better than the Romer-Romer projections had implied, vindicating Keynesian fiscal theory comprehensively
The fiscal multiplier was exactly 1.5 as predicted and the unemployment outcome was within the projected range, with the 10% peak being attributable to mid-2009 demographic factors only
The fiscal multiplier was negative because of crowding-out effects, with the ARRA actually causing the unemployment increase rather than dampening it, a finding endorsed by mainstream economics
questions.context: The Romer-Romer projections were public in early 2009. The actual outcome was substantially worse. The episode is often cited (Cochrane, Cogan, Taylor, Wieland) as evidence that headline-Keynesian multipliers overstate fiscal stimulus efficacy. The 2020-21 stimulus produced inflation rather than the predicted output gains — another data point in the same direction.

questions.question: Central-bank independence became a fashionable institutional-design principle in the 1980s-90s. The argument: politicians have short horizons and pressure central banks to inflate before elections, so insulating monetary policy from democratic accountability protects long-run price stability. Bundesbank, RBNZ (1989), BoE (1997) became models. What does the capture critique add?
questions.answer: Independence from elected officials still leaves central banks captured by the financial sector they regulate, swapping political accountability for industry capture rather than eliminating it
choices: Independence from elected officials still leaves central banks captured by the financial sector they regulate, swapping political accountability for industry capture rather than eliminating it
Central-bank independence has fully solved the problem of monetary capture and there are no remaining concerns about whose interests independent central banks actually serve in any practice
Central banks are not independent in practice and are still directly controlled by elected officials, making the 1980s-90s institutional reforms cosmetic changes with no measurable effects at all
Industry capture of central banks has no measurable effect on monetary policy and the concept of regulatory capture does not apply to central banking under any reasonable definitional analysis
questions.context: Stigler 1971 'Theory of Economic Regulation' is the foundational text. The Fed-Treasury-Wall Street revolving door (Rubin, Paulson, Geithner, Yellen) is the canonical example. Independence from voters is not the same as independence from concentrated economic interests.

questions.question: The Fed-Treasury-Wall Street revolving door is structural to US financial policymaking. Robert Rubin: Goldman Sachs to Treasury Secretary to Citigroup (where he received ~$115M while Citigroup needed bailouts). Hank Paulson: Goldman CEO to Treasury Secretary in the 2008 crisis. Janet Yellen: Fed Chair to Treasury Secretary. What concern does this raise?
questions.answer: The same people who set policy go on to high-paying positions at firms benefiting from those policies, distorting incentives toward favorable treatment for future employers
choices: The same people who set policy go on to high-paying positions at firms benefiting from those policies, distorting incentives toward favorable treatment for future employers
The revolving door has no measurable effect on policy decisions and the same officials would make identical choices if their post-government careers were restricted by binding contractual rules
The revolving door is a media fiction and former Treasury Secretaries rarely take private-sector positions after government service, instead retiring to academic or charitable roles afterward
The revolving door flows in one direction only, with private-sector executives entering government but never leaving for private positions, so concerns about bias are unfounded as a result
questions.context: The pattern is bipartisan. Geithner: Treasury to NY Fed President to Treasury Secretary to Warburg Pincus president. The Rubin-Paulson-Geithner-Yellen sequence concentrated bailout-determination power in a small social network. Public choice predicts and explains the pattern.

questions.question: Greece joined the euro in 2001. The 2010 sovereign-debt crisis exposed long-running fiscal deficits hidden by Goldman Sachs currency-swap accounting. Greek bond yields spiked to 30%+ in 2012. The 'troika' (ECB, European Commission, IMF) imposed austerity for bailouts totaling ~286 billion euros. The 2015 Tsipras referendum rejected the conditions but Syriza accepted them anyway. What did the crisis reveal?
questions.answer: A currency union without a fiscal union is structurally unstable; countries cannot devalue out of crises and are locked into politically explosive internal-deflation adjustments
choices: A currency union without a fiscal union is structurally unstable; countries cannot devalue out of crises and are locked into politically explosive internal-deflation adjustments
The eurozone is perfectly stable and the Greek crisis was caused by Greek fiscal misbehavior with no structural eurozone design flaws contributing to the persistence of the recession
The eurozone was secretly dissolved in 2015 and replaced with a new currency arrangement, with the Greek crisis being the publicly visible portion of a larger institutional restructuring
Greece left the eurozone in 2015 after the referendum and adopted a new drachma, with the eurozone continuing to function without Greek membership from that point onward in monetary history
questions.context: Robert Mundell's 'optimum currency area' theory (1961) anticipated the eurozone's structural problem decades before. The political failure to act on the theory's implications is the deeper story. The euro survived; the contradiction did not resolve. Italy, Spain, and France carry the risk forward.

questions.question: On July 26, 2012, ECB President Mario Draghi told a London conference: 'Within our mandate, the ECB is ready to do whatever it takes to preserve the euro. And believe me, it will be enough.' Italian and Spanish bond yields fell sharply over following weeks. Draghi never had to deploy the OMT (Outright Monetary Transactions) program in size. What did the speech reveal?
questions.answer: A credible threat of unlimited intervention can move markets without requiring intervention, but only when the central bank has both legal authority and political backing to follow through
choices: A credible threat of unlimited intervention can move markets without requiring intervention, but only when the central bank has both legal authority and political backing to follow through
Central-bank verbal interventions have no measurable effect on markets and the Italian and Spanish bond yield declines after July 2012 were caused entirely by unrelated supply-and-demand factors
Draghi was forced to deploy massive bond purchases immediately after the speech and the 'whatever it takes' line was a coincidence rather than a market-moving event in eurozone history that year
The ECB had no authority to make the statement and Draghi was personally censured by the European Council for exceeding his mandate, with the speech being formally repudiated within only weeks
questions.context: The German Constitutional Court eventually challenged the OMT framework but never invalidated it. The 'whatever it takes' speech is studied as a canonical case of rhetorical central-banking. The deeper question (whether the underlying contradictions are merely deferred) remains open through Lagarde.

questions.question: Fed Chair Jerome Powell spent most of 2021 calling the post-COVID inflation 'transitory'. By November 30, 2021, he retired the word. The Fed began raising rates in March 2022 (25bps), then 50bps in May, then four 75bps hikes through November. The funds rate reached 4.25-4.50% by year-end, from 0 in March. What does the 2021-22 sequence illustrate?
questions.answer: Central banks systematically underestimate inflation when political-economic incentives favor accommodation, and only act decisively once the political cost of inaction exceeds the cost of recession
choices: Central banks systematically underestimate inflation when political-economic incentives favor accommodation, and only act decisively once the political cost of inaction exceeds the cost of recession
Central banks are accurate forecasters of inflation and the 2021 'transitory' framing was correct since inflation did eventually return to target levels by the end of the disinflation cycle in 2023
Central banks have no incentive to underestimate inflation and Powell's 2021 statements reflected the best available macro models without any political or institutional bias toward accommodation
Central banks always act preemptively against inflation and the 2021-22 sequence was an exception caused by unusual COVID-era data noise that misled an otherwise highly responsive monetary framework
questions.context: The 'transitory' framing aged poorly. Summers's February 2021 warning and other Austrian and monetarist warnings preceded the Fed's recognition by about a year. The delay shows up in the 9.1% peak inflation and the savings of fixed-income households eroded during that period.

questions.question: From December 2008 through December 2015 the Fed held the federal funds rate at 0-0.25% (Zero Interest Rate Policy, ZIRP). Real rates were negative for much of the period. Asset prices rose strongly. Saving in bank deposits earned negative real returns. What is the Austrian recognition about a sustained near-zero rate regime?
questions.answer: Persistent below-natural rates distort capital allocation, encourage debt accumulation, inflate asset prices, and tax savers who provide the real capital the economy needs for productive investment
choices: Persistent below-natural rates distort capital allocation, encourage debt accumulation, inflate asset prices, and tax savers who provide the real capital the economy needs for productive investment
Persistent near-zero rates have no distributional consequences and produce identical outcomes for savers and asset holders, with the wealth gap remaining unchanged through any monetary policy regime
Persistent near-zero rates eliminate the business cycle by smoothing investment over time and are recommended as permanent policy by Austrian economists for that reason in their academic writings

The 2008-15 ZIRP period had no measurable effect on US asset prices and the strong equity-market rally during this time was driven entirely by improved corporate fundamentals unrelated to monetary policy
questions.context: The ZIRP era's distributional consequences (asset-holders won, savers and renters lost) became a major political issue in the 2016 election. The Fed's policy frame focused on aggregate employment without giving distributional weight to the Cantillon-effect transfer the policy enacted.

questions.question: The ECB under Mario Draghi introduced negative interest rates on bank reserves in June 2014. The Bank of Japan went negative in January 2016. By 2019 about $17T in global sovereign debt traded at negative yields, with investors paying governments to hold money. The policies aimed to force banks to lend rather than hoard reserves. What did the NIRP era reveal?
questions.answer: Below-zero rates produced limited extra lending and substantial financial-sector distortion (margin compression, asset bubbles, currency competition) without delivering promised growth
choices: Below-zero rates produced limited extra lending and substantial financial-sector distortion (margin compression, asset bubbles, currency competition) without delivering promised growth
Negative interest rates have been an unqualified success in stimulating economic growth and are now permanent policy in the eurozone and Japan with widespread support from economists today
Negative interest rates had no measurable effect on financial markets or lending behavior and were essentially cosmetic policies adopted by central banks for political-signaling purposes for years
Negative interest rates caused immediate hyperinflation in the eurozone and Japan, which is why both central banks abandoned the policy within months of introduction without any sustained NIRP period
questions.context: The NIRP era prompted a wave of 'why hold cash in a bank' analyses and indirectly contributed to Bitcoin's institutional adoption. The Swiss National Bank's deeper negative rates (-0.75% peak) were a particularly stark case. NIRP was abandoned across most jurisdictions in the 2022-23 hiking cycle.

questions.question: The BoJ pioneered modern unconventional monetary policy beginning the early 2000s. QE ran 2001-2006, then relaunched as 'Quantitative and Qualitative Easing' (QQE) under Governor Kuroda from April 2013 with a 2% inflation target. The BoJ became Japan's largest holder of government bonds and a major equity-ETF holder. Inflation hit 2% only briefly. What did Japan teach?
questions.answer: Open-ended QE can suppress yields and elevate asset prices for years without sustained inflation in a high-savings society, at the cost of central-bank balance-sheet dominance over markets
choices: Open-ended QE can suppress yields and elevate asset prices for years without sustained inflation in a high-savings society, at the cost of central-bank balance-sheet dominance over markets

QE always produces immediate hyperinflation regardless of underlying economic conditions, and the Japanese experience contradicted basic monetary theory in ways that have never been adequately explained
QE has no measurable effect on any economic variable and the Japanese experiments with unconventional policy 2001-2024 had no consequences for Japanese asset prices or for the yen exchange rate
The BoJ abandoned QE in 2010 after concluding it had no effect on inflation, and Japanese monetary policy returned to conventional interest-rate management for the entire post-2010 period since
questions.context: The BoJ's experience anticipated much of the post-2008 Fed and ECB toolkit. The 'Japanification' thesis (slow growth, falling labor force, deflation, central-bank dominance) was applied to Europe and floated for the US. The 2024 BoJ rate normalization is the first serious test of unwinding the regime.

questions.question: AIG was the world's largest insurer in 2008. Its Financial Products division had written ~$440B in CDS protection on mortgage-backed securities. As securities lost value, AIG faced margin calls it could not meet. On Sept 16, 2008 (one day after Lehman), the Fed gave an $85B bridge loan; bailout reached $182B. About $100B flowed to counterparties at 100 cents on the dollar. Who benefited?
questions.answer: Goldman Sachs ($12.9B), Societe Generale, Deutsche Bank, Merrill Lynch, and other major banks that got full payment on CDS contracts they would have collected pennies on in bankruptcy
choices: Goldman Sachs ($12.9B), Societe Generale, Deutsche Bank, Merrill Lynch, and other major banks that got full payment on CDS contracts they would have collected pennies on in bankruptcy
The bailout funds flowed primarily to retail insurance policyholders who would otherwise have lost their life-insurance and annuity benefits if AIG had filed for bankruptcy through normal courts
The bailout funds were returned to the US Treasury immediately and no private firms received any payments from AIG's federally provided bridge loan during the entire 2008-2010 financial crisis period
AIG counterparties received only partial payment on CDS contracts and the haircuts were similar to what an ordinary insurance-company liquidation would have produced for similar creditors
questions.context: The 'backdoor bailout' framing came from this counterparty-payment detail. The bailout was technically a loan to AIG, but the cash went almost immediately to AIG's counterparties at par. The structure shielded the recipients from any creditor haircut.

questions.question: The FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee) sets US monetary policy. It has 12 voting members: 7 from the Board of Governors (presidential appointees, Senate-confirmed) and 5 from the 12 regional Fed Banks (NY Fed permanent; 4 rotate). The regional banks are technically private corporations owned by member commercial banks. What does this structure mean institutionally?
questions.answer: Monetary policy is set by a body partly composed of representatives from privately owned regional banks owned by commercial banks, blending public and private authority in ways unique to federal agencies
choices: Monetary policy is set by a body partly composed of representatives from privately owned regional banks owned by commercial banks, blending public and private authority in ways unique to federal agencies
The Federal Reserve is a fully public agency with no private-bank participation in its policy decisions, and the 12 regional Fed Banks are simply subsidiary offices of the federal government itself
The Federal Reserve is a fully private corporation with no government oversight at all, and the Board of Governors is appointed by member banks rather than by the President of the United States
The FOMC has no authority to set US monetary policy, which is determined by the US Treasury, with the FOMC providing only ceremonial advisory opinions during their regular meetings
questions.context: The hybrid structure is intentional: Aldrich Plan to Glass-Owen kept the regional-bank private-corporate framing for political reasons. Member commercial banks elect 6 of the 9 directors at each regional Reserve Bank. The 'public agency wearing private clothes' nature is why public choice applies.

questions.question: The Federal Reserve Reform Act of 1977 amended the Federal Reserve Act to give the Fed a 'dual mandate': maximum employment AND price stability. (A 'moderate long-term interest rates' goal is nominally included.) Before 1977, the Fed had no explicit congressional mandate. Why does the dual mandate create internal tension other central banks (Bundesbank, RBNZ, BoE) avoid?
questions.answer: Price stability and full employment can conflict short-run, so the Fed must trade them off without explicit congressional guidance, leaving room for political pressure and discretion
choices: Price stability and full employment can conflict short-run, so the Fed must trade them off without explicit congressional guidance, leaving room for political pressure and discretion
Price stability and full employment never conflict and the dual mandate creates no policy tensions, with the Fed always able to pursue both goals simultaneously without any institutional difficulty
Other central banks have identical dual mandates and the Fed's institutional position is no different from the Bundesbank, RBNZ, or post-1997 Bank of England in any meaningful structural dimension
The 1977 Reform Act has been repealed and the Fed no longer has any explicit congressional mandate, returning to its pre-1977 status of being free to set its own goals without statutory direction
questions.context: Bundesbank (pre-euro), RBNZ (1989), and BoE (1997) all moved to single-mandate (price stability) designs explicitly to escape the dual-mandate tension. The US dual mandate is consistently invoked to defend looser policy in slowdowns. The 2021-22 inflation surge restarted the long-running debate.

questions.question: Mortgage securitization (Fannie Mae 1968 reform, Freddie Mac 1970) transformed home loans from bank-held assets into tradable bonds. By the mid-2000s, private-label MBS (mortgage-backed securities) packaged subprime loans, sold to global investors as AAA-rated. Credit rating agencies (Moody's, S&P, Fitch) collected fees from issuers. What was the structural problem?
questions.answer: Originators no longer held the loans they made, so credit standards collapsed; rating agencies were paid by issuers, so AAA ratings were systematically inflated for fee income
choices: Originators no longer held the loans they made, so credit standards collapsed; rating agencies were paid by issuers, so AAA ratings were systematically inflated for fee income

Mortgage securitization improved credit standards by spreading risk and the 2008 crisis was caused entirely by unrelated factors with no contribution from the securitization process or rating agencies
Mortgage securitization was banned by the SEC in 2002 and the 2008 crisis involved no MBS issuance, with the entire collapse being caused by ordinary bank lending without any market-based instruments
Mortgage securitization was managed entirely by the federal government with no private-sector involvement, and the 2008 crisis was a pure governmental policy failure with no role for private actors
questions.context: Michael Lewis's The Big Short (2010) and the FCIC Report (2011) document the structural-incentive failures. The Cassandras (Michael Burry, Greg Lippmann, Steve Eisman) saw it coming; the institutional mainstream did not. Friedrich Hayek's epistemic-failure framework explains the pattern.

questions.question: Bernie Madoff was arrested December 11, 2008 after his sons reported him to the FBI. The Ponzi scheme had run since the 1990s, defrauding investors of ~$65B in claimed assets (~$19B in real losses). Harry Markopolos had warned the SEC repeatedly since 2000; the SEC investigated five times and found nothing. Madoff got 150 years. What does the case illustrate about regulatory capture?
questions.answer: Markopolos's mathematical proof that Madoff's returns were impossible was ignored by SEC staff lacking technical capacity and institutional incentive to act against a well-connected insider
choices: Markopolos's mathematical proof that Madoff's returns were impossible was ignored by SEC staff lacking technical capacity and institutional incentive to act against a well-connected insider
Markopolos was wrong about Madoff and the SEC investigations were correct in finding no fraud, with the eventual 2008 collapse caused by unrelated market conditions during the financial crisis
The SEC acted quickly on Markopolos's warnings and shut down Madoff in 2002, with the 2008 arrest being a separate matter unrelated to the earlier Ponzi-scheme allegations entirely
Madoff was not running a Ponzi scheme and the 2008 arrest was based on accounting errors since reversed, with the $65 billion in losses being a media exaggeration of routine market losses
questions.context: Markopolos's No One Would Listen (2010) details the failed warnings. Madoff was the former NASDAQ chairman with deep social ties to SEC officials. The case is a canonical example of regulatory capture compounded by competence gaps.

questions.question: Glass-Steagall (Banking Act of 1933) separated commercial banking (deposit-taking, lending) from investment banking (underwriting, trading), in response to Depression-era bank failures. The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act of 1999 repealed key sections, allowing financial holding companies to combine activities. Citigroup formed from Travelers + Citibank ahead of repeal. What is the argument linking repeal to 2008?
questions.answer: Combination let large banks use insured deposits to fund speculative trading, spread losses across the system, and made firms large enough to require bailouts when they failed
choices: Combination let large banks use insured deposits to fund speculative trading, spread losses across the system, and made firms large enough to require bailouts when they failed
Glass-Steagall repeal had no measurable effect on the 2008 crisis and was unrelated to any aspect of the system collapse, with the crisis being caused entirely by housing prices alone
Glass-Steagall was strengthened in 1999 rather than repealed, and the system in 2008 was substantially more separated than it had been in 1933 under FDR's New Deal program
Glass-Steagall repeal was rolled back in 2005 and was not in effect during the 2008 crisis, with the underlying institutional framework being identical to the pre-repeal 1933 structure
questions.context: Clinton signed Gramm-Leach-Bliley with Treasury Secretary Larry Summers's support. Robert Rubin later joined Citigroup, becoming the canonical example of the revolving door. Post-2008 Dodd-Frank did not restore Glass-Steagall's separation.

questions.question: The Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act (July 21, 2010) was the largest financial-regulatory overhaul since the New Deal. It created the CFPB, FSOC, Volcker Rule, and imposed enhanced capital requirements. By 2024 the largest US banks were larger than in 2008. What does Dodd-Frank illustrate?
questions.answer: Complex regulatory frameworks tend to entrench the largest incumbents who can afford compliance costs, creating barriers to entry that consolidate the industry the regulation was supposed to discipline
choices: Complex regulatory frameworks tend to entrench the largest incumbents who can afford compliance costs, creating barriers to entry that consolidate the industry the regulation was supposed to discipline

Dodd-Frank successfully broke up the largest banks and the post-2010 financial system has many more small institutions than the pre-crisis system did, restoring competitive banking conditions in the US
Dodd-Frank has been entirely repealed and the post-2008 financial-regulatory framework is identical to the pre-2008 framework, with no Dodd-Frank-era requirements remaining in effect anywhere today
Dodd-Frank had no measurable effect on bank concentration and the 2010-2024 increase in large-bank market share was caused entirely by unrelated demographic and technology factors with no role
questions.context: Public-choice theory predicted this outcome: incumbent firms shape regulation in their favor, and 'reform' often increases industry concentration rather than disciplining it. The Stigler 1971 capture framework explains the pattern. The 2023 SVB-Signature episode showed mid-tier banks remain vulnerable.

questions.question: Silicon Valley Bank failed on March 10, 2023, the second-largest US bank failure ever. SVB held ~$200B in assets; ~95% of deposits were above the FDIC $250K insurance cap. SVB had loaded up on long-duration Treasuries during 2020-21, then took mark-to-market losses as Fed rate hikes pushed bond prices down. The run completed in 24 hours via Twitter and digital banking. What did regulators do?
questions.answer: Treasury, Fed, FDIC invoked a 'systemic risk exception' to backstop ALL deposits (including uninsured), setting a precedent that raises the FDIC cap to infinity for large banks
choices: Treasury, Fed, FDIC invoked a 'systemic risk exception' to backstop ALL deposits (including uninsured), setting a precedent that raises the FDIC cap to infinity for large banks
Regulators applied standard FDIC rules and depositors with balances above $250K lost the uninsured portion of deposits, consistent with the pre-2023 framework for bank failures in the US
Regulators allowed SVB to recover without intervention and the bank continued operating normally after March 2023, with no federal action being required to stabilize the institution
Regulators nationalized SVB and the federal government continues to own the bank as of 2024, with no private-sector resolution of the March 2023 failure having taken place to date
questions.context: Signature failed the same weekend; First Republic in early May; all received the systemic-risk treatment. Credit Suisse failed days later (UBS shotgun marriage backed by Swiss central bank). 'Too big to fail' expanded to 'too large to lose deposits' regardless of size or politics.

questions.question: The 12 regional Federal Reserve Banks are technically owned by their member commercial banks, which must subscribe to stock equal to 6% of their capital and surplus. Members receive a 6% statutory dividend on paid-in stock. Member-bank shareholders elect 6 of the 9 directors of their regional Reserve Bank. Why does this matter for public-choice analysis?
questions.answer: Direct ownership and director-election rights give member banks formal channels of influence on monetary policy the public lacks, embedding industry capture in the institution's legal structure
choices: Direct ownership and director-election rights give member banks formal channels of influence on monetary policy the public lacks, embedding industry capture in the institution's legal structure
Member-bank ownership is purely ceremonial and member banks have no influence over Fed policy through any formal or informal channels in the modern Federal Reserve System operating today
Member banks do not own Fed regional banks and the FOMC is composed entirely of presidential appointees with no industry representation, making the institution structurally insulated from capture
Member banks are owned by the Federal Reserve rather than the reverse, with regional Fed Banks holding equity stakes in member commercial banks rather than the other way around structurally
questions.context: The structure dates to 1913 Glass-Owen as a political compromise: bankers wanted private control, populists wanted federal control, the hybrid satisfied neither but endured. The 6% dividend is paid out of Fed earnings before any remittance to the US Treasury.

questions.question: Irving Fisher (1867-1947), the Yale monetary economist, proposed in 100% Money (1935) that commercial banks be required to hold 100% reserves against checking deposits. Credit creation would be separated from deposit-taking. Frank Knight, Henry Simons, and other Chicago economists endorsed the plan. The Chicago Plan was floated in 1933 and rejected. What does the proposal target?
questions.answer: Fractional-reserve banking's instability: banks create deposit money via loans, expanding the money supply pro-cyclically and amplifying boom-bust cycles the central bank then tries to manage
choices: Fractional-reserve banking's instability: banks create deposit money via loans, expanding the money supply pro-cyclically and amplifying boom-bust cycles the central bank then tries to manage
The 100% reserve plan was not about banking and was instead a proposal for reforming the gold standard with no relation to fractional-reserve deposit creation or monetary-amplification effects
The Chicago Plan was adopted in 1933 and US banks have operated under 100% reserve requirements ever since, making fractional-reserve banking illegal in the US from the New Deal onward

Fisher's plan was a Marxist proposal for nationalizing all banks and the Chicago economists endorsing it were sympathizers of central planning, making the entire idea opposed to free-market principles
questions.context: Murray Rothbard endorsed 100% reserves (with gold rather than paper) as the Austrian sound-money ideal. Mises and Hayek were more divided. Modern proposals (Kotlikoff's 'Limited Purpose Banking', Turner's narrow banking) revisit Fisher's framework. 2008 GFC reawakened the debate.

questions.question: Bretton Woods (July 1944) created the IMF and the IBRD (later the World Bank). The IMF would lend to countries running balance-of-payments difficulties; the World Bank would fund postwar reconstruction and later development. Both bodies were headquartered in Washington under US influence. What does the architecture reveal?
questions.answer: The postwar monetary system was designed as much for US geopolitical leadership as for monetary stability; the institutions' DC location and dollar-centricity embed US power in the global framework
choices: The postwar monetary system was designed as much for US geopolitical leadership as for monetary stability; the institutions' DC location and dollar-centricity embed US power in the global framework
The IMF and World Bank were designed as neutral technocratic institutions with no special relationship to US geopolitical interests and have been independent of US influence ever since 1944
The Bretton Woods institutions were never actually created and the postwar monetary system functioned without any formal international bodies until the 1971 Nixon shock dissolved the arrangement
The IMF and World Bank were headquartered in Geneva rather than Washington, and the postwar monetary system was designed to give equal influence to all 44 founding nations regardless of size
questions.context: The IMF managing director is by tradition European; the World Bank president is by tradition American. The institutions' 'structural adjustment' lending (Africa, Latin America, post-Soviet states) became deeply controversial in the 1990s-2000s. Austrian economists are largely critical.

questions.question: The Marshall Plan (1948-1951) provided ~$13.3B (~$170B in 2024 dollars) in US aid for Western European reconstruction. The program is credited with rapid postwar recovery in West Germany, France, Italy. The German Wirtschaftswunder, often attributed to the Plan, owed more to Ludwig Erhard's 1948 currency reform and free-market liberalization. Why does the distinction matter?
questions.answer: Foreign aid can support recovery only when domestic policies (property rights, sound money, free markets) make productive use of resources; aid without reform produces dependency
choices: Foreign aid can support recovery only when domestic policies (property rights, sound money, free markets) make productive use of resources; aid without reform produces dependency
Foreign aid is sufficient on its own to produce economic recovery regardless of domestic policies, and the Marshall Plan demonstrated this principle which has been confirmed in every subsequent case
The Marshall Plan was actually a failure and West German recovery happened despite the program rather than because of it, with the postwar economic miracle being explained by other factors entirely
The Marshall Plan was the only factor in West German recovery and Erhard's 1948 currency reform had no measurable effect on the economic outcome of the postwar period in Germany or elsewhere
questions.context: Ludwig Erhard, Hayek-influenced and Austrian-aligned, abolished price controls and replaced the Reichsmark with the Deutsche mark in June 1948 against Allied skepticism. Eastern Europe's postwar trajectory is the counterfactual: same aid offered Stalin refused, opposite institutional choices.

questions.question: On June 20, 1948, Ludwig Erhard, economics director of the British-American Bizone, abolished postwar price controls and replaced the worthless Reichsmark with the new Deutsche mark at 10:1. Allied authorities had not approved the price-control liberalization; Erhard acted on his own. Within days, shop windows filled with hoarded goods. Black markets collapsed. What does this demonstrate?
questions.answer: Markets respond rapidly to sound money and free prices; the German postwar miracle began with a 24-hour shock that ended scarcity by ending the price controls and currency debasement causing it
choices: Markets respond rapidly to sound money and free prices; the German postwar miracle began with a 24-hour shock that ended scarcity by ending the price controls and currency debasement causing it
Markets respond slowly to policy changes and the German recovery took a decade to begin, with the 1948 currency reform having no measurable effect during the first years after its enactment
Markets respond only to fiscal stimulus and the 1948 currency reform had no economic effect, with German recovery being driven by Marshall Plan aid disbursed over the subsequent years
The 1948 currency reform was never implemented and the Reichsmark remained Germany's currency until the introduction of the euro in 2002, with no Deutsche mark issuance taking place in 1948
questions.context: Wilhelm Roepke (Hayek-aligned Austrian) was Erhard's intellectual influence. The Allied authorities tried to fire Erhard for unauthorized action; he could not be fired because he was technically not under their authority. The episode is a clean test of Hayekian arguments about markets, prices, and information.

questions.question: In February 2022, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the US Treasury froze ~$300B in Russian central-bank reserves held at the Fed and ECB. The action was unprecedented: reserves had traditionally been treated as sovereign-immune. The dollar's reserve-currency status depends on this immunity. What did the freeze signal to other central banks?
questions.answer: Holding reserves in any currency exposes the issuer to political risk if relations sour; the action sped up central-bank gold buying and dollar-alternative discussion among BRICS nations
choices: Holding reserves in any currency exposes the issuer to political risk if relations sour; the action sped up central-bank gold buying and dollar-alternative discussion among BRICS nations

The freeze had no signaling effect on other central banks and global reserve allocation has remained unchanged since 2022, with no measurable increase in central-bank gold purchases or dollar diversification

The freeze actually increased dollar demand because other central banks viewed it as evidence of US monetary strength, and dollar reserve share rose to record highs in the years following the 2022 sanctions
The Treasury reversed the freeze in months and Russian reserves were returned in full, with no consequences for the dollar's reserve-currency status or for central-bank confidence in US commitments
questions.context: Central-bank gold purchases reached record levels in 2022-23. China, India, Turkey, and various Gulf states accelerated diversification. The deeper question (whether the dollar's reserve role is being slowly eroded) remains open. The freeze was a calculated weapon; the long-run cost may exceed the short-run gain.

questions.question: The Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930 raised US tariffs on over 20,000 imported goods to the highest levels in over a century. Over 1,000 economists signed a petition urging Hoover to veto. He signed it. Global trade fell about 65% between 1929 and 1934. What does Smoot-Hawley illustrate about protectionism?
questions.answer: Tariffs invite retaliation from trading partners, collapsing the cross-border specialization that gains-from-trade depends on, deepening rather than relieving the downturn that motivated the protection
choices: Tariffs invite retaliation from trading partners, collapsing the cross-border specialization that gains-from-trade depends on, deepening rather than relieving the downturn that motivated the protection

Tariffs always increase domestic employment and output, and Smoot-Hawley successfully protected US industry through the 1930s with no measurable negative effects on the US economy or its trading partners
Smoot-Hawley had no measurable effect on global trade and the 1929-1934 trade decline was caused entirely by unrelated demographic and currency factors with no link to US tariff policy
Smoot-Hawley was repealed in 1931 before having any effect and the 1930s decline in trade volume happened without any tariff barriers being in effect at any point in any major economy
questions.context: Senator Reed Smoot (R-Utah) and Representative Willis Hawley (R-Oregon) championed the bill at the protectionist edge of the GOP. The 1000-economist petition was organized by Paul Douglas. Hoover signed despite the warning. Trade collapsed; the protected industries did not survive. Lessons widely ignored in subsequent tariff debates.

questions.question: Beginning 2018, the Trump administration imposed tariffs on Chinese imports under Section 301, covering ~$370B in goods at 7.5-25% rates. China retaliated, particularly hitting US agricultural exports. The 2020 Phase One deal partially de-escalated. Studies (Amiti et al., Fajgelbaum et al.) found the tariffs were passed through to US consumers and producers. What does the episode show?
questions.answer: Tariffs are paid by domestic consumers and producers rather than by foreign exporters; the 'China is paying' framing was contradicted by every serious analysis of pass-through
choices: Tariffs are paid by domestic consumers and producers rather than by foreign exporters; the 'China is paying' framing was contradicted by every serious analysis of pass-through
Tariffs are paid by foreign exporters as Trump claimed, and the 2018-19 tariffs successfully transferred wealth from China to the United States with no cost to US consumers or businesses
The 2018-19 tariffs had no measurable economic effects and were entirely symbolic, with US prices and trade flows unchanged from pre-tariff baselines throughout the entire post-2018 period
The 2018-19 tariffs were not actually implemented and the Section 301 action was a media story without any actual policy effect on US-China trade flows in any year during the Trump term
questions.context: The Biden administration largely maintained the Trump tariffs through 2024. Both parties moved toward protectionism. The Phase One deal's purchase commitments were not met. The political appeal of 'tough on China' framings outran the economic analysis of who actually pays the tax.

questions.question: In 1845 Frederic Bastiat published 'The Petition of the Candle Makers', a satirical petition to the French Chamber of Deputies demanding protection from 'unfair competition' from a foreign rival, the sun. The candle makers argued blocking sunlight would create jobs for candle makers, shutter makers, oil producers. Bastiat's reductio was meant to expose what?
questions.answer: Every protectionist argument can be applied to any competitor, including the sun; if 'creating jobs' justifies tariffs, it justifies any restriction however absurd, exposing the underlying fallacy
choices: Every protectionist argument can be applied to any competitor, including the sun; if 'creating jobs' justifies tariffs, it justifies any restriction however absurd, exposing the underlying fallacy
The petition was a sincere proposal from the French candle industry and was actually adopted by the Chamber of Deputies, with sunlight being restricted in France for several decades afterward

The petition argued for free trade with the sun and against protection of the candle industry, with Bastiat actually supporting tariffs against foreign manufactured goods despite his satirical framing

The petition was a serious economic analysis showing that sunlight competition really did hurt the French candle industry and that protection was a legitimate policy response to international solar trade
questions.context: Bastiat's 'The Candlemakers' Petition' is anthologized in 'Economic Sophisms' (1845). The satire is one of the clearest expositions of the seen-and-unseen fallacy applied to trade. The candlemakers' argument structure recurs in every modern industry-protection lobby — exposed by Bastiat 180 years ago.

questions.question: New York City has had rent control or rent stabilization since 1943, originally as a wartime measure. The Rent Control Law of 1947 made it permanent. By 2024 ~half of NYC apartments are rent-stabilized. Studies (Glaeser, Diamond) find the policy reduces tenant mobility, lowers maintenance, distorts allocation, and reduces new construction. What does this illustrate?
questions.answer: Rent control transfers wealth to current tenants while damaging future renters, current landlords, and the city's housing supply, so seen benefits concentrate while unseen costs spread broadly
choices: Rent control transfers wealth to current tenants while damaging future renters, current landlords, and the city's housing supply, so seen benefits concentrate while unseen costs spread broadly
Rent control benefits all New Yorkers equally and has no distributional consequences, with the policy being supported by virtually all New York economists across schools as good housing policy
Rent control was repealed in NYC in 1970 and the city has operated under purely free-market housing arrangements ever since, with no rent control on any units in any borough as of 2024
Rent control causes housing supply to increase by encouraging development of unregulated units, with NYC having one of the highest per-capita housing construction rates among major US cities now
questions.context: Assar Lindbeck (Swedish socialist economist) once said 'in many cases rent control appears to be the most efficient technique presently known to destroy a city, except for bombing.' The literature is one of the strongest cross-school consensuses in applied economics.

questions.question: Sweden has the strictest rent regulation of any developed economy. New tenants in Stockholm wait up to 20 years for a regulated apartment. The black market for sublet rent-controlled units is large. Most new tenancies happen through informal swaps, family transfers, or under-the-table payments. Why does Sweden's textbook case persist politically?
questions.answer: Current beneficiaries (sitting tenants in regulated units) vote on existing leases while future tenants do not yet have apartments, so the public-choice asymmetry favors visible winners over invisible future losers
choices: Current beneficiaries (sitting tenants in regulated units) vote on existing leases while future tenants do not yet have apartments, so the public-choice asymmetry favors visible winners over invisible future losers
Sweden has no housing shortage and the rent regulation works perfectly with no waiting lists, no black markets, and no informal allocation systems anywhere in Stockholm or other Swedish cities at all
Sweden abolished rent regulation in 2010 and the country now has a fully free housing market, with the apparent shortage in Stockholm being caused entirely by unrelated immigration policy decisions
Sweden's rent regulation is supported by Austrian economists as a model for sound housing policy, with the Mises Institute publishing a 2018 monograph praising the Swedish system as exemplary
questions.context: Sweden's Stockholm waiting list reached 20+ years in some areas by the 2010s. Assar Lindbeck and Stefan de Vylder (Swedish economists) have written critically. The political durability across left-right governments illustrates how regulation creates its own political constituency that defeats reform.

questions.question: San Francisco voters passed Prop H in 1979, expanding rent control to most apartment buildings built before 1979. Rebecca Diamond et al.'s 2019 American Economic Review study examined long-run effects: protected tenants got lower rents but new construction declined sharply, and landlords converted controlled buildings to condos. What was the net distributional finding?
questions.answer: Protected tenants gained roughly $2.9B but housing-supply contraction transferred similar or greater costs to future renters who couldn't find apartments and paid higher market rents
choices: Protected tenants gained roughly $2.9B but housing-supply contraction transferred similar or greater costs to future renters who couldn't find apartments and paid higher market rents
Protected tenants gained $2.9B at no cost to anyone else, with the housing supply unchanged and no measurable effects on rents in unregulated buildings throughout San Francisco's market history
Protected tenants lost money on the policy because their reduced mobility prevented them from accepting higher-paying jobs elsewhere in California, with no benefits to anyone in any group as a result
Diamond et al. found no measurable effects of Prop H on any rental-market variable and recommended further expansion of rent control as a costless policy across other California cities to follow
questions.context: Diamond et al. used administrative data to track individuals over time. The empirical literature consistently finds rent control reduces supply and reallocates rather than creates wealth. The 2019 AER paper is the most-cited modern study of US rent control effects.

questions.question: Berlin's Senate passed the Mietendeckel (Rent Cap) law in February 2020, freezing rents at June 2019 levels and rolling back recent increases. New supply collapsed within months. On April 15, 2021, the German Federal Constitutional Court struck down the law, ruling Berlin lacked authority. Rents bounced back sharply. What does the episode illustrate?
questions.answer: Even short-term rent freezes produce measurable supply distortions; the political will to impose such measures shows the public-choice durability of the policy temptation regardless of evidence
choices: Even short-term rent freezes produce measurable supply distortions; the political will to impose such measures shows the public-choice durability of the policy temptation regardless of evidence
The Mietendeckel was a great success and would have solved Berlin's housing shortage if not for the Federal Constitutional Court's politically motivated decision to strike down a popular policy
The Mietendeckel had no measurable effect on Berlin housing during its 14 months of operation, with new construction unchanged from pre-2020 baselines throughout the entire 2020-2021 period

The Mietendeckel is still in effect as of 2024 and Berlin operates under the most successful rent-control regime in Europe, with the German Constitutional Court ruling being widely disregarded by Berlin authorities
questions.context: The Berlin SPD-Greens-Linke coalition pushed the Mietendeckel through despite expert testimony that it would reduce supply. Construction permits for new apartments collapsed during the law's brief effective period. The episode is a textbook case of policy ignoring evidence under public-choice pressure.

questions.question: David Card and Alan Krueger's 1994 AER paper studied NJ's 1992 minimum wage rise ($4.25 to $5.05) versus neighboring PA. Their phone-survey method found no employment decline at fast-food restaurants. The result was widely cited as overturning textbook predictions. Neumark-Wascher 2000 used payroll records and found significant declines in the same data. What does this show?
questions.answer: Empirical results depend heavily on data sources and method; the highest-quality data (payroll records) confirmed the textbook prediction that minimum-wage increases reduce employment
choices: Empirical results depend heavily on data sources and method; the highest-quality data (payroll records) confirmed the textbook prediction that minimum-wage increases reduce employment
Card-Krueger is the definitive empirical study and proved that minimum-wage laws have no employment effects, with all subsequent studies confirming the result without further academic contradiction
Both studies used identical data and methodology, with Card-Krueger and Neumark-Wascher results being identical and uncontroversial within the empirical labor-economics literature ever since 1994
Card-Krueger was retracted by the American Economic Review in the 1990s and is no longer considered a legitimate source for any minimum-wage policy discussion in academic economics anywhere
questions.context: Card later won the 2021 Nobel partly for the natural-experiment methodology. Neumark and Wascher's payroll-record critique is the canonical methodological rebuttal. The popular framing 'Card-Krueger settled it' is misleading; the underlying economics question remains active.

questions.question: Seattle phased in a $15 minimum wage between 2015 and 2017. The University of Washington's NBER team (Jardim et al. 2017) used administrative payroll data and found low-wage workers' total hours fell by about 9%, with average earnings DOWN about $125/month despite the higher hourly rate. The Berkeley team found smaller effects using county-level QCEW data. What is the contrast?
questions.answer: When researchers can see actual worker-level hours, the predicted employment effects appear; when researchers use aggregated data missing the part-time and hours-cut adjustments, effects are diluted
choices: When researchers can see actual worker-level hours, the predicted employment effects appear; when researchers use aggregated data missing the part-time and hours-cut adjustments, effects are diluted

The UW and Berkeley studies were identical in methodology and findings, with both research teams concluding the Seattle minimum wage had no adverse effects on workers or businesses anywhere in the city
The UW study was retracted in 2018 after methodological errors were discovered, with the Berkeley study being the only reliable evidence on the Seattle minimum-wage policy outcome to date
The Berkeley study was retracted in 2018 after methodological errors were discovered, with the UW study being the only reliable evidence on the Seattle minimum-wage policy outcome to date
questions.context: The Jardim et al. NBER paper used administrative payroll data from the Washington Employment Security Department. The Berkeley team used Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages data that aggregates and masks the worker-level adjustments. The methodological gap explains the result gap.

questions.question: The CBO's minimum-wage analyses (2014, 2019, 2021) consistently find a positive employment effect for workers who keep their jobs at higher pay AND a negative effect for workers priced out. The 2021 analysis of a $15 federal minimum estimated 1.4M job losses against pay raises for 17M. What is the CBO's framework?
questions.answer: Minimum-wage policy is a redistribution from workers priced out of jobs to workers who keep them at higher pay; the policy question is whether that trade-off is worth making, not whether there are losers
choices: Minimum-wage policy is a redistribution from workers priced out of jobs to workers who keep them at higher pay; the policy question is whether that trade-off is worth making, not whether there are losers
Minimum-wage policy has no employment effects in any direction and the CBO has consistently found no measurable impact on the labor market from any minimum-wage proposal it has analyzed historically
Minimum-wage policy benefits all workers equally and the CBO has found no losers from any minimum-wage proposal, with the 1.4M job-loss figure being a media misrepresentation of CBO findings entirely
Minimum-wage policy harms all workers equally and the CBO has found no winners from any minimum-wage proposal, with the 17M pay-raise figure being a media misrepresentation of CBO findings entirely
questions.context: The CBO's methodology integrates the empirical literature into a structural model. The 2021 estimates for a $15 federal minimum drew criticism from both directions. The honest Bastiat framing (seen wage gains, unseen jobs lost) is built into the analysis even when political deployment downplays one side.

questions.question: Ricardo's 1817 comparative advantage shows two countries gain by specializing even when one is more efficient atything. Modern critics (Reinert, Chang) note the static model ignores transition costs, learning-curve effects, network externalities. Trump-era industrial policy debates revived the question of whether developing-country tariffs can build industries comparative advantage would never grow. What is the honest summary?
questions.answer: Comparative advantage is correct as a static gains-from-trade result but doesn't address dynamic questions of how productive capacity is built; both static gains and dynamic concerns are real
choices: Comparative advantage is correct as a static gains-from-trade result but doesn't address dynamic questions of how productive capacity is built; both static gains and dynamic concerns are real
Comparative advantage is a complete theory of all trade dynamics and the dynamic concerns raised by Reinert and Chang have no empirical or theoretical merit anywhere
Comparative advantage is false and Ricardo's 1817 paper was retracted by the Royal Economic Society in the 1900s, with all modern trade theory rejecting his framework
Comparative advantage applies only to agricultural goods and was never intended for industrial or manufactured products, with industrial-policy debates being outside Ricardo's intended scope
questions.context: Bastiat's 1840s candle-makers satire targeted static protection. Modern industrial policy debates (Reinert, Chang) revisit dynamic questions Ricardo set aside. The Austrian position emphasizes voluntary exchange but acknowledges Hayek's spontaneous-order insights apply more naturally to free trade than to managed development.

questions.question: Leonard Read's 1958 essay 'I, Pencil' tells the autobiography of an ordinary pencil. The pencil notes that no single person knows how to make a pencil: graphite from Sri Lanka, cedar from Oregon, rubber from Malaysia, copper from Chile, paint, lacquer, brass for the ferrule. Thousands of unrelated people cooperate via the price system without any central plan. What does Read's essay illustrate?
questions.answer: Hayekian spontaneous order: complex production emerges from voluntary exchange without any central authority understanding the whole, because prices coordinate dispersed knowledge into cooperation
choices: Hayekian spontaneous order: complex production emerges from voluntary exchange without any central authority understanding the whole, because prices coordinate dispersed knowledge into cooperation
Central economic planning is necessary for the production of pencils, and Read's essay was a tongue-in-cheek argument FOR centralized industrial policy rather than against it
The Foundation for Economic Education (publisher) retracted 'I, Pencil' in the 1970s after concluding pencils cannot actually be produced without central planning by a government agency anywhere
Read's essay is a Marxist allegory about alienated labor in industrial production, with the pencil representing the worker estranged from the means of production
questions.context: Read founded the Foundation for Economic Education in 1946. 'I, Pencil' was popularized further by Milton Friedman's video segment in Free to Choose (1980). The essay is the canonical short illustration of Hayek's 1945 knowledge-problem argument made concrete and memorable. Russ Roberts updated it in 2012.

questions.question: Hayek's 'spontaneous order' (Greek: kosmos) describes complex systems that emerge from voluntary interactions without central design: language, common law, money, scientific discovery, internet protocols. The deliberately-designed alternative (taxis) often fails because no designer has the information needed. What is the political-economic implication?
questions.answer: Many of civilization's most important institutions are products of human action but not of human design, so the impulse to replace them with consciously planned systems usually destroys more than it builds
choices: Many of civilization's most important institutions are products of human action but not of human design, so the impulse to replace them with consciously planned systems usually destroys more than it builds
All complex social institutions are products of deliberate central design and Hayek's spontaneous-order distinction is a Romantic fiction in social or economic history
Spontaneous order applies only to physical sciences and has no relevance to political-economic institutions, with all economic systems requiring conscious design
Hayek argued that spontaneous orders are inferior to planned orders and recommended that all social institutions be replaced with deliberately designed alternatives wherever practical or possible
questions.context: Adam Ferguson's 'Essay on the History of Civil Society' (1767) anticipated the concept. Hayek's 1973 'Law, Legislation and Liberty' developed kosmos/taxis systematically. The framework explains markets, common law, language, and (in Bitcoin) digital money.

questions.question: James Buchanan won the 1986 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences for his work on public choice — applying economic methodology (rational self-interest, marginal analysis) to political institutions.
